title: Live: Adam Reynolds sidelined for Lang Park farewell against Storm
text:
(Getty)

The NRL is taking its chance in some of these dead rubber games between non-finals teams to trial a new kick-off rule.

The new rule gives the a team that concedes a try the option to kick off or receive after their opponents score.

This rule, which brings the game closer to American football, was initially floated before the season and roundly pilloried as somewhere between pointless and a terrible idea, prompting the league to pull out.

But now they get their chance to see it in action, and I look forward to seeing both teams choose to receive the ball after being scored on all night, until the last moment of the match where one team chooses to kick off because why not at that point.

Literally the only scenario I can imagine where a team who's just conceded a try would choose to kick off rather than receive would be if there's only seconds on the clock and they're down by one or two, so they want to try a short kick-off to hopefully regather and rapidly kick a field goal.

title: Matildas follow Socceroo footsteps on path to World Cup
text:
The Matildas are looking to follow the Socceroos' blueprint when they play in next year's FIFA Women's World Cup, and two friendlies against Colombia will be a key stepping stone.

On Thursday the Matildas announced they will play the first of two games against the South American giants on November 28 at Canberra Stadium.

The date and venue of the second clash are yet to be determined.

The matches will be an invaluable warm-up ahead of next year's World Cup, which kicks off in Brazil on June 24, with the final on July 25.

And the Matildas, who finished fourth at the 2023 World Cup co-hosted by Australia and New Zealand, are keen to set up the team for long-term success.

With current players including Sam Kerr, Steph Catley, Emily van Egmond and Mackenzie Arnold entering the latter stages of their careers, there are concerns about the Matildas missing such a wealth of talent and experience once they retire.

Heather Garriock, Football Australia's executive director of football, said the friendlies against Colombia would make sure younger players are prioritised.

"We sat down with (coach) Joe (Montemurro) some 12 months ago when he started in the Matildas position, and we asked him what his ideal preparation was in the lead-up to the Women's World Cup," Garriock said on Thursday.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

"It was very evident that different styles of play were important to him, but also trying to blood some of the next generation as well.

"We've seen that (younger players getting an opportunity) at the recent World Cup in the US with (Socceroos coach) Tony Popovic as well.

"Joe's style is very creative, very structured and process-driven."

The Socceroos' next generation shone at this year's World Cup in North America, with Nestory Irankunda, Alessandro Circati and Lucas Herrington subsequently earning contracts with major European teams.

The success of the Socceroos' young squad members came after Popovic integrated rising talent into the side in the lead-up to the tournament.

The Matildas are hoping to follow that blueprint, and 21-year-old goalkeeper Chloe Lincoln says getting game time in friendlies against top nations will help her confidence heading into Brazil.

"Playing them (Colombia) at the She Believes Cup, we got a sense of their style, and it's an amazing opportunity to (play) that opposition," Lincoln said.

"Now that the A-League is kicking off again, there's more opportunity for the local players and some of the younger girls playing in that competition to really put … their names forward.

"Especially in these friendly matches, every match really counts, building cohesiveness as a group and working on how we want to perform over in the World Cup."

title: Move to slash amount of vitamin B6 considered safe by 72 per cent
text:
Months after taking vitamin supplements, Dominic Noonan-O'Keefe says he feared he was dying.

His body was overwhelmed by pain and numbness, his mind overcome with dread.

"Every millimetre of my body was exploding with misfiring, misdirected signals to my brain," he told 7.30.

"There were lightning bolts through my body 24 hours a day. It was the most awful thing I've ever lived through."

Dominic Noonan-O'Keefe says he still lives with symptoms after cutting vitamin B6 out of his diet. (Supplied: Dominic Noonan-O'Keefe)

Today, more than two years after he stopped taking the supplements, he said the pain had "turned down", but he still lived with balance and vision problems, among a long list of symptoms he attributes to unknowingly consuming too much vitamin B6.

Amid a public health crackdown, Australia's peak health research body is moving to cut the amount of vitamin B6 considered safe to consume.

The medicines regulator has also confirmed it will act within weeks to bring in stronger warnings and labelling, as consumers are urged to check what is in their cabinets.

Proposed change to 'upper limit'

Vitamin B6 is an essential nutrient found naturally in foods like meat, fish and vegetables.

But the synthetic form, also known as pyridoxine, is added to thousands of products sold in Australia — from supplements like multivitamins, B-complex tablets, magnesium and zinc tablets, to fortified foods and drinks including protein powders, energy drinks and weight-loss shakes.

The amount of vitamin B6 considered safe has been revised down by the National Health and Medical Research Council. (ABC News: Tom Hartley)

Since 2006, regulators, doctors and manufacturers have all worked from the same figure: the intake of up to 50 milligrams of vitamin B6 a day was safe.

That threshold is known as the "upper limit".

But after an extensive review of global evidence, Australia's peak health research body, the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC), has now recommended reducing it by 72 per cent to 14mg.

"There's really no good reason to be taking 50mg of vitamin B6, unless of course you're suffering from severe malnutrition," said Tim Green, who co-chaired the working group behind the proposed change.

The amount of B6 people are advised to consume for good health — around 1.3mg a day — is not changing.

Professor Green said a deficiency would be rare.

Vitamin B6 is often found in fortified foods like some breakfast cereals and bread. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

"It wouldn't happen with a normal Australian diet," he said.

Matt Silsby, a neurologist and neurophysiologist, said B6 toxicity typically caused "primarily sensory symptoms, pins and needles or prickling or painful symptoms", and sometimes cramps or muscle twitches.

In more serious cases, he said it could "get quite severe and lead to nerve damage", and in a subset of those patients that damage can be permanent.

He was quick to stress that symptoms "could potentially have very many causes", and it's "not appropriate to just attribute everything to the vitamin B6 level".

Regulators, manufacturers face potential shake-up

The review followed years of mounting concern and, recently, a dramatic intervention by the medicines regulator.

In November last year the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) — which had conceded it had been too slow to act — moved to pull high-dose B6 products from general sale, while also asking the NHMRC to review the science behind the limit.

According to the recommendation, the new limit would apply to all adults, including during pregnancy and breastfeeding, with lower limits for children scaled down by body weight, to as little as 4mg a day for under-4s.

Alexandra Jones, a food policy expert at the George Institute for Global Health, told 7.30 the proposed reduction was "encouraging" and brought Australia "closer to the approach adopted by the European Food Safety Authority", which enforces some of the most conservative safety limits in the world.

Alexandra Jones says the proposed reduction of vitamin B6 levels is "encouraging". (ABC News: Craig Hansen)

The upper limit is also a key reference that medicine and food regulators draw on when deciding what can be sold, how it is labelled, and what sits behind the pharmacy counter.

"The outcomes of the NHMRC's work are not regulatory, but they do provide an important scientific foundation for updating guidance to consumers and potentially updating policy and regulation down the track," Dr Jones said.

The working group acknowledged the change could carry "cost implications for manufacturers", but said its decision was "made on the basis of population health".

" There's nobody who's going to be harmed by lowering it," Professor Green said, "but there will be people who may be harmed by keeping it at 50 milligrams. "

'Hidden' in supplements and energy drinks

Just how many Australians have been affected is impossible to say.

Pathology clinics across the country sounded the alarm more than a year ago, noting a spike in concerning results.

But the TGA's surveillance of cases has been cumbersome.

The TGA publicly lists reports of potential issues related to medicines as "adverse events". As of August 13, the current number of potential peripheral neuropathy cases linked to pyridoxine (B6) since 2020 was 279.

But even by the TGA's own admissions, that number should not be considered an accurate reflection of prevalence in the community.

The Australian lobby group for complementary medicines, CMA, which represents major manufacturers, maintains that adverse events are "extremely rare".

A CMA spokesperson told 7.30 "high doses of vitamin B6 are often recommended by healthcare practitioners for specific therapeutic benefits or preventing deficiency".

Professor Green believes toxicity cases are under-reported and what has been recorded officially was "likely the tip of the iceberg", probably skewed towards the most "severely affected people".

Vitamin B6 is found in supplements like multivitamins, B-complex tablets, magnesium and zinc tablets. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts )

Another issue in trying to understand prevalence is that toxicity symptoms exist on a spectrum and can often mimic other conditions.

Dr Silsby, who is researching the effect of B6 on nerves, said patients rarely realise how much they are taking and were often "absolutely shocked" when they figured out how many of their products contain B6.

"It can be hidden or unexpected in supplements … and we always ask them to go home and check through their cabinets and to stop anything that contains it," he said.

Professor Green himself admitted he unknowingly took B6 in a magnesium supplement for a while.

"If I can't figure it out, having been in this area for 20 years, how is the general public meant to?" he said.

For many people, though, the biggest source of hidden B6 is not vitamin supplements.

The NHMRC working group's analysis found that in 2023, nearly a third (32.9 per cent) of Australians' dietary vitamin B6 intake came from just three sources: electrolyte, energy and fortified drinks; cereal-based dishes like sandwiches and pasta; and poultry — but noted the latter two groups contain too little B6 to be a concern.

Energy drinks like these can contain high levels of Vitamin B6. (ABC News: Cameron Lang)

Dr Jones said the revised limit was "yet another good reason for energy drink consumers to rethink that habit".

While individual drinks are in the safe range of vitamin B6, problems could potentially arise if people consume multiple products containing synthetic B6.

"A single can of a popular energy drink can contain around 5 milligrams," she said, "so those drinking multiple cans, and particularly those combining energy drinks with supplements, need to take note."

But while the NHMRC offers advice, the rules governing what goes into foods and drinks are set separately by Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ).

Dr Jones told 7.30 the onus should not be on consumers "to maintain vigilance and read the fine print on everything," and said FSANZ should "consider updating guidance on an appropriate 'one day quantity' and potentially limiting the content of B6 permissible in energy drinks".

FSANZ said it would "carefully consider the final outcomes and any implications for food regulation", once a final recommendation was accepted.

The Australian Beverages Council, whose membership includes energy drink manufacturers, said it was consulting members over the proposal and would "comply with any relevant regulatory changes".

It noted the TGA's review had found supplements, not drinks, to be the largest source of dietary B6.

Complementary Medicines Australia — which represents about 80 per cent of the sector — played down the significance of the recommended change, noting the new figure is a dietary guideline, not a rule for medicines, and that supplements already carry warning labels and follow the regulations.

Previous safe limit set on 'biased' evidence

The NHMRC group behind the recommendation included toxicologists, pharmacologists, neurologists, a chemical pathologist, a GP, public health experts and a specialist in complementary medicines, as well as a member with lived experience of B6 toxicity.

An external review commissioned found the evidence behind the old 50mg figure was thin, resting largely on small, decades-old overseas studies that carried a "high risk of bias".

There had never been much solid data to work from, Professor Green said, because proper studies would mean deliberately harming people.

Tim Green believes vitamin B6 toxicity cases are under-reported. (Supplied)

"People don't normally set out to poison people in studies," he told 7.30, adding that some of the earlier research would be considered "unethical" by modern standards.

What had changed, he said, was how much B6 people now consume, often without knowing, driven by the proliferation of supplements in recent years.

"The more people you start exposing to supplements, the more things that are going to come up that you didn't expect," he said, explaining that the committee primarily considered mounting adverse-event reports and recent international guidance, to "err on the side of caution."

The 'slow cogs' of progress

Mr Noonan-O'Keefe told 7.30 the NHMRC's recommendation was "fantastic" and "going in the right direction", and hoped the TGA was paying close attention.

"I hope they look at this latest body of evidence, which has existed for a long time, and recognise the level of action they've taken to date is insufficient," he said.

Dominic Noonan-O'Keefe wants the TGA to act quickly on the new recommendation. (Supplied: Dominic Noonan-O'Keefe)

Under the TGA's current settings, products containing up to 50mg of vitamin B6 will remain on general sale until at least June 2027, more than three times the dose the new science says is safe.

In a statement to 7.30, the TGA said it had run a successful public safety campaign earlier this year and said "in the coming weeks" it intended to consult on further measures —including stricter labelling, as well as lowering the threshold at which products must carry a warning about nerve damage.

But the TGA spokesperson wouldn't commit to "further regulatory action", including considering scheduling changes, until the final NHMRC recommendations process was complete.

"A time frame for this work has not been decided," the spokesperson said.

That wait is hard to accept for people living with the consequences of toxicity.

"What are we waiting for?" Mr Noonan-O'Keefe said.

"A working group has established the issue, so the regulator knows and we expect them to be swift — not slow-turning cogs."

The NHMRC proposal is open for public submissions until September 30, with a final decision expected next year.

From there it would be up to the regulators to decide whether what's on the shelves should more closely match the recommendation.

title: Bill granting 'extraordinary powers' to speed up development passes parliament
text:
A controversial bill granting the Queensland government significantly expanded compulsory acquisition powers has passed state parliament.

The new law allows for projects to be declared "state strategic" by the government, meaning projects can be streamlined through a suite of new powers granted to the coordinator-general.

The State Development and Public Works Organisation (Critical Minerals) and Other Legislation Amendment Bill (2026) is touted by the government as essential for the state to capitalise on the critical-minerals boom.

A map of critical mineral deposits in Queensland. (Supplied: Department of Natural Resources and Mines, Manufacturing and Regional and Rural Development)

Critics of the bill, which passed through parliament on Wednesday night, said it put too much power in the hands of the planning minister and eroded fundamental legal safeguards.

Significantly, the bill allows for the government to acquire land for private projects for the first time.

The bill also weakens appeal rights and allows for other legislation to be edited through new "modification orders".

The Crisafulli government said the powers would not automatically allow a project's approval or remove existing environmental, planning, resources, or other approval requirements.

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said the bill was aimed at securing investment in critical minerals.

"This legislation gives us the tools to attract investment, create jobs and build new industries," he said.

"There's billions of dollars on the table."

Critical minerals are materials the state government describes as being crucial for modern economies and are at risk of supply chain disruption.

Deposits in Queensland include vanadium and cobalt for batteries, and copper for electrical, renewable and digital infrastructure.

Late amendments

Queensland's agriculture industry was a vocal critic of the bill, airing concerns that prime agricultural land would be taken for mining, renewable energy and tourism projects.

The day the bill passed, amendments were added that excluded renewable energy projects and data centres from being declared state strategic.

Amendments were also made to ensure a Regional Interests Development Approval (RIDA) was still required.

A RIDA is a separate legislation used to protect areas of special economic interest, including agricultural land.

Shane McCarthy is happy with the amendments made to the Critical Minerals Bill. (ABC Rural: Brandon Long)

AgForce Queensland president Shane McCarthy said he negotiated with the government right up until the last minute.

"They have taken on some of our recommendations … we would have preferred it to go a little bit further, but you never get [all of what you] asked for," he said.

"It's great to see a government that actually listens and takes on board what their regional constituents are saying."

Queensland Farmers Federation CEO Kylie Porter said she believed the legislation was aimed at achieving balance.

"Legislation is one piece, but we also now need to make sure that our proponents of critical minerals are really acting in a way that's very appropriate for the interests of our agriculture community," she said.

'No meaningful safeguards'

Environmental Defenders Office Queensland managing lawyer Andrew Kwan said the late amendments failed to address the bill's central flaws.

"These amendments add no meaningful safeguards, tighter eligibility criteria or greater transparency and accountability around the use of these extraordinary powers," Mr Kwan said.

"In the face of climate change and continued environmental decline in Queensland, major projects must face robust assessment and public scrutiny, not unjustified fast-tracking or weakened legal protections."

Critics said that while critical minerals were important, nothing in the bill restricted the powers to govern just critical-mineral projects.

Kylie Porter welcomes the passage of the amended legislation for the state's primary producers. (ABC News: Cathy Van Extel)

In July, Mr Bleijie used the $140 million Whitsunday Skyway cable-car project between Airlie Beach and Conway National Park as an example of a project that could be expedited under the law.

Pascale Whyte lives near the proposed cable-car base station site and is disappointed the law has passed.

"What this bill does is flip the basic Queensland principle of a fair go on its head," she said.

"It gives a commercial tourism project, complete with a luge track, the same fast-track powers as a critical mine, and it strips away the safeguards that let everyday residents be heard.

"That's not streamlining, that's overriding our community's rights."

The Skyway project has not been declared a state strategic project.

Conservation groups protested across the state last week, calling the new legislation an overreach that put the environment and land rights at risk.

title: NSW couple confirmed missing in deadly Nepal floods
text:
The ABC has confirmed the identity of a NSW couple who are among a tour group including 15 Australians currently missing in Nepal after catastrophic flash flooding.

Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and his wife Chitra Venkatraman, 46, from Western Sydney, were taking part in a tour with US-based hiking company Himalayan Glacier when the natural disaster struck.

Nepal flash floods updates: Follow as this story as it unfolds with our live blog.

The couple's son told the ABC he last spoke to his parents when they were approximately 15 kilometres from the Tibet border.

He said he had not heard from them since, but he held out hope the entire tour group would be found safe.

"I'd like to see my parents and everyone who went with them back in one piece, and that everyone else there is as safe as possible," he said.

Hundreds of foreign nationals have been reported missing after flash floods in Nepal. (AP: Niranjan Shrestha)

The tour company said a group of 47 people, including the 15 Australians, were still unaccounted for in the Langtang Valley.

Two Australian boys, aged 11 and 14, are also part of the tour group.

Queensland mother-of-two among missing

Swaatika Kanniah is the daughter of missing tourist Kanagamah Sundrasan, who visited Mount Kailash to complete a pilgrimage.

"According to her itinerary, today was supposed to be the day she was getting there, basically," Ms Kanniah said.

"It's a very sacred spot, so it was one of her dreams to fulfil."

Kanagamah Sundrasan had visited Mount Kailash to complete a pilgrimage. (Supplied)

The mother-of-two owns a business with her husband in Queensland, and last spoke to her family on Tuesday.

"It's been a bit worrying because we haven't been able to contact her yet; it's been really hard to grab hold of anyone who has any information," Ms Kanniah said.

" We really want her to come back home and we miss her, like, a lot. "

Ms Kanniah said her mum was "very giving" and "the kindest woman ever".

"She doesn't really go on trips like this; that's why it was very exciting for her to travel and do this thing that she always wanted to do."

Anxious wait for loved ones living in Australia

Dipendra Bistra was confirmed missing by his sister-in-law, who lives in Adelaide. (Supplied)

In Adelaide, Manisha Khatri is anxiously awaiting news about her missing brother-in-law Dipendra Bistra.

Ms Khatri found out Mr Bistra was unaccounted for during a routine call to family on Wednesday night.

"They have a little daughter around three years old. They just started their life and now he's gone missing," she said.

Ms Khatri said there was nothing she could do but pray.

"There is a different kind of pain in watching, like, our home country and homeland drown while we are miles away," she said.

"We are unable to express our feelings; it hurts."

Foreign Minister Penny Wong said the "scale of the destruction is devastating".

She said she had been in contact with Australia's ambassadors in Nepal and China to offer her support and request that they do "everything they are able" to help locate missing Australians.

Travellers in the area are being advised to exercise caution and follow the advice of local authorities.

title: A GST deal and the NDIS blew out by billions — but one is sacred
text:
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where this week Jake Evans will get you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.

Former prime minister Scott Morrison must have been surprised when he was asked by a reporter in 2022, a few months before the federal election, whether he had "neglected" Western Australia.

Morrison, as treasurer, had stitched up a deal in 2018 to guarantee WA a larger slice of the pie from the Goods and Services Tax (GST), which he said would cost the federal budget about an extra $5 billion over about six years.

The Coalition had been facing a political backlash in WA, where the mining state's share of revenue from the GST had slipped to 30 cents for every dollar collected because its high iron ore royalties changed the calculation for what the state was owed.

Morrison promised the federal government would top-up WA so that it always received a "floor" of at least 75 cents for every dollar it raised, which he expected would cost the federal budget an extra $5.4 billion.

Politically, it didn't matter in the end.

Scott Morrison promised the federal government would top-up WA so that it always received a "floor" of at least 75 cents for every dollar it raised, which he expected would cost the federal budget an extra $5.4 billion. (ABC News: Nick Haggarty)

The Coalition's gift to the west in 2018, dubbed the worst deal in policy history by economists like Saul Eslake, didn't save the Liberal Party from losing five seats in WA at the 2022 election — four of those to Labor, which had made a vow written in sharpie to keep the GST deal.

Eight years on, the $5 billion gift to WA has instead cost $23 billion, and is expected to cost $60 billion by 2030.

Escape plan from 'costly' WA GST deal The Productivity Commission finds the WA GST deal is a "costly mistake" that has led to "perverse" outcomes, and recommends it be scrapped.

Undertaking a review at the government's request, the Productivity Commission advised the deal should be scrapped, calling it a "costly mistake" that was worsening inequality between the states.

It was a rare moment since Morrison's deal that gave cause for critics to hope there could be a slim chance of change.

But that was quickly extinguished, as the prime minister looked the $60 billion blow-out in the eye and vowed once again to keep it.

Standing next to him was West Australian Premier Roger Cook, who had earlier in the month insulted Productivity Commission public servants as "clowns", "dodgy, deceitful" and "dumb".

Treasurer Jim Chalmers later defended them as "really good people", and said Cook's remarks were "unfortunate".

But the prime minister said nothing of Cook's comments, suggesting an "economic rationalist" viewpoint was to be expected from a Productivity Commission report commissioned by a Coalition government.

Never mind the fact the Albanese government appointed the Productivity Commissioner and wrote the terms of reference for its GST report.

Albanese, who credits the swing in the west with delivering him the prime ministership in 2022, is refusing to create an opening for a Liberal (or One Nation) revolt in WA.

But angry premiers are warning it could start costing Labor votes among the "clowns" outside WA.

South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas told the Bush Summit his constituents had begun to ask him about the deal. (ABC News: James Wakelin)

South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas told the Bush Summit this morning his constituents had begun to ask him about the deal.

"You can win every single seat in every single seat in Western Australia, but if you don't win a majority of seats in the rest of the country, you still lose," Malinauskas said.

The GST deal is a blowout as big as the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS), which was on course to cost about $70 billion a year by 2030, tens of billions more than projected at its inception.

Health Minister Mark Butler announced earlier this year the government had made the difficult choice to force some people from the scheme to state-run alternatives, and cut the budgets of others, in order to save about $38 billion over four years and finally slow down growth to a sustainable rate.

"These reforms will help make the NDIS safer, clearer and more sustainable, with stronger rules, better safeguards and greater confidence that funding is directed to the supports participants need," Butler said at its passage last week.

With the federal budget cash-strapped, in deficit for the next ten years, and the "low-hanging" savings picked already, the government and Coalition were able to find agreement last week to cut back on an expense item costing tens of billions more than first expected.

It just wasn't the one that's been dubbed "the worst deal in policy history".

Energy Minister Chris Bowen on Sunday said the government was ready to ride roughshod over the Queensland and Northern Territory governments. (ABC News: Dave Sciasci)

More head-butting at national cabinet

It has been a turbulent week for Labor.

Energy Minister Chris Bowen on Sunday said the government was ready to ride roughshod over the Queensland and Northern Territory governments to see through its plan to force AI data centres to use renewables power to neutralise the massive increase in energy consumption that the data centre rush is forecast to bring.

This morning, it was Queensland Premier David Crisafulli and NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro doing a victory lap after forcing a federal government backdown to a "technology agnostic" approach that would allow data centres to still use coal and gas to make their AI-generated deepfakes of Alan Kohler.

The government insists it wasn't a backdown — Environment Minister Murray Watt this morning said the government recognised "some states and territories that are in a different situation with state-owned generation".

It seems to be somewhat academic, since the three big data centre states are shaping up to be NSW and Victoria by a wide margin, and South Australia coming in third, all where renewables are full steam ahead.

There's little suggestion data centre developers are waiting in the wings with plans to support a new coal project that would get their facilities on line.

And no government or opposition, federal, state or territory, wants to be the one that killed the golden goose of AI, which promises to bring in more than $100 billion in value over the next decade.

But in a fight between data centres and renewables yesterday, it was data centres that won.

Loading

Disunity in the rank-and-file

Within Labor, there are fissures from a commitment to cut down migration levels by nearly 100,000 to a net overseas arrival rate of 225,000 by 2028.

The political squabble over the most appropriate Net Overseas Migration rate tripped up One Nation's most junior MP, David Farley, at the beginning of the week, when he likened the party's migration plans to Labor's, and suggested a figure that would be "at minimum" slightly higher than the federal government's target.

His leader Pauline Hanson came over the top to clarify in a tweet a few hours later, confirming the party's policy was to cut net migration to 130,000.

Four days on it is all clear as mud, with Hanson saying today the party's migration target will in fact be above the 130,000 she had previously suggested, though Farley was also "confused" about how certain visa holders were counted — the Coalition is saying Hanson took three different positions in about as many minutes.

But the government is hardly handling it more neatly.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke was forced to postpone a scheduled National Press Club address, as the government's planned changes to cut down arrivals to reach its target of 225,000 hit a snag.

It hasn't been settled in the several cabinet meetings since, and there is no date pencilled in the calendar for the announcement.

With the migration debate a daily occupation, and according to a Sydney Morning Herald poll the single-largest issue driving the One Nation-curious, some policy proposals have found their way into the headlines.

After the ABC reported a government plan to make British backpackers work a stint in the country in order to make the popular visa less attractive, the prime minister quickly squashed the suggestion at a press conference yesterday — sealing one escape route for the government to reach its migration target.

Then a proposal to cut the nation's humanitarian intake by allowing a four-year lift from 13,750 visas to 20,000 to expire caused fury within Labor's left faction, national affairs correspondent Jane Norman reported, with the left faction feeling it had ceded enough ground on the issue of asylum seekers and refugees.

Labor had only just settled to keep that visa at 20,000 places at its national conference a few weeks earlier.

The prime minister, responding to the Australian Financial Review's report of the proposal, said not to believe "everything you read in the Fin".

But was it reporters or his own MPs he was telling that to?

The answer to that question came through late on Thursday, with a confirmation from the prime minister to the ABC the humanitarian intake would be staying at 20,000 — one less lever the government can pull.

title: Minimum security wing unused for a decade despite prison overcrowding
text:
A minimum-security wing at one of Western Australia's newest prisons has remained unused for a decade, despite inmates in other sections of the jail allegedly sleeping on the floor because of overcrowding.

Unit 5 is a minimum security facility located outside the secure perimeter fence at Eastern Goldfields Regional Prison in Kalgoorlie-Boulder, about 600km east of Perth.

The $232 million prison opened 10 years ago this month and was described at the time as the "jewel in the crown in the WA prison estate" by then-corrective services minister Joe Francis.

The entrance to Eastern Goldfields Regional Prison. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

But Unit 5 has never been used, which the Department of Justice attributed to "staffing issues".

It is the latest saga in the state's under-fire corrections system after the ABC this month revealed prisoners were receiving financial compensation to sleep on the floor in overcrowded jails.

Inmates 'sleeping on floor'

WA Prison Officers' Union secretary Andy Smith said Unit 5 has nearly 100 beds and claimed some prisoners at the Boulder jail are sleeping on mattresses on the floor due to overcrowding, a claim the department denies.

"There are prisoners on the floor in Kalgoorlie … at this point in time, it's probably around 20, but that's 20 too many," he said.

WA Prison Officers' Union secretary Andy Smith says there is a shortage of prison officers across the state. (ABC News)

"Unit 5 was purpose-built for community work, so that prisoners could be external to the fences and put back into the community.

"They've never been able to staff the prison sufficiently enough to open it, and in fact, the prison runs short of staff on a daily basis."

He said the state was short of 1,200 prison officers in total.

The department blames staffing woes for the unit being unused. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

The department said the prison housed 330 inmates as of Tuesday, below its capacity of 367.

It denied any prisoners were sleeping on the floor but did not provide staffing numbers, which the union claims are dangerously low.

When the prison was built, the department signed a 25-year maintenance contract with contractor Honeywell.

A prison officer secures a cell door at Eastern Goldfields Regional Prison. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

"It means the government pays for the upkeep of that unit, so for the last 10 years, the department has been paying the contractor to maintain Unit 5, even though there has never been a prisoner in there," Mr Smith said.

"There is an allowance for repainting it, replacing equipment like beds and mattresses et cetera, and it's never been touched, so the upkeep on that portion of the prison is huge and it's never been used."

Inspection report due

The Inspector of Custodial Services was due to conduct an inspection of Eastern Goldfields Regional Prison in May, but its findings are yet to be presented to parliament.

Its 2023 inspection found the prison was staffed for 310 prisoners, with 18 out of 111 prison officer positions vacant.

"Resolving the staffing issues could mean up to 100 beds would be available to be brought online to relieve population pressure on the adult male estate," the 2023 audit found.

"One of the key elements of the staffing issue is retention rather than recruitment."

To help boost staffing, the department said eligible prison officers and their dependents were being offered free rent and significant mortgage assistance.

title: The numbers behind Carlton's transition from AFLW darling to contender
text:
Carlton was the darling of the AFLW last year.

It returned to the finals for the first time since 2020, pressed toward a preliminary final, and challenged perennial contender Brisbane on its home deck.

The fear — especially in the AFLW — is that the comedown the following year is hard and fast for those sides that propel themselves up the ladder.

Short seasons, a heavily weighted fixture list, and small playing roster sizes prone to injuries, can all make linear growth far harder to come by. But the Blues have bucked that trend in a big way to start the 2026 season.

Instead of coming into the year expecting to do the same thing, albeit with more experienced players, the Blues have adapted their game style further.

They have tapped further into what worked last year but also added new layers that prove the coaching panel's willingness to look toward future trends of the game.

The handball game

Carlton is moving the ball fast on the run, including handballs, from a midfield featuring Claudia Whitfort. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Where in 2025 the Blues moved the ball by foot 61.3 per cent of the time, that has dropped way back in 2026 to 54.4 per cent. In turn, their handball metres gained have shot through the roof from 178 metres per game last year, to an average of 335 across the opening two rounds this season.

This has also driven an AFLW-wide growth in the area, with teams across the league working to get the ball forward by hand more often, but the Blues' growth is far ahead of any other side at this stage.

Unsurprisingly, this has seen Carlton's average handballs go from 100.8 last year, to 134.0 this year and, importantly, it is hitting its targets more reliably.

Much of this is built on the midfield trio of Mimi Hill, Abbie McKay, and recruit Claudia Whitfort.

Carlton's ball movement by hand 2025 2026 Average handballs 100.8 134.0 Average handballs metres gained 178.0 335.0 Average kick rate percentage 61.3 54.4 Average inside 50s 35.5 37.5

By moving the ball with speed, on the run, hitting those handball receive options, the Blues are getting the ball forward more consistently than they ever have before.

Transition footy

Last year a pillar of Carlton's growth was its improved rebounding from defensive 50, and capacity to turn opposition forward entries into their own scoring chains.

That has only grown this year off the back of that handballing transition game.

They have scored +51 points from turnover — the greatest differential in the AFLW across the opening fortnight — and have scored more points from defensive 50 score launches than any other side, at 33 points.

Their rebound rate has increased year on year, as has their score from the back half.

Carlton's growing transition game 2024 2025 2026 Average points from D50 launches (AFL rank) 0.3 (last) 8.6 (1st) 16.5 (1st) Average rebound rate percentage 78.7 82.5 85.5

The solid defensive trio of Harriet Cordner, Ciara Fitzgerald, and Maddy Hendrie established itself last year, so now with Irishwoman Siofra O'Connell added to the line, Cordner has a little more freedom to get off a direct opposition and kickstart much of the attack.

All-Australian and Carlton best and fairest winner Dayna Finn is also a crucial part of this defensive transition, as is Amelia Velardo who has locked down a mid-sized defensive role this year thanks to consistency with her body and role.

A different way to attack

To finish off their work, the biggest change this year has been what the Blues do once inside 50. Last year a reliance on marking targets close to goal was found — Tara Bohanna, Sophie McKay, and Breann Harrington were the main targets in this respect.

This year, that has totally changed. Harrington is sitting out the season while pregnant with her first child, and Bohanna is finding it hard to make it into the team.

So, instead of playing that marking game, the Blues are using space and ground-level forwards to do the damage on the scoreboard.

Nell Morris-Dalton (R) leads the Carlton goalkicking with four goals this season, as marks inside 50 have dropped away. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

The inclusion of Nell Morris-Dalton as, ostensibly, the key forward target and a supporting cast of smaller forwards around her, has made the Blues harder to defend against.

But the only way this works is thanks to the faster movement up the ground to isolate those players on the deck in goal-side space.

So, while Carlton's marking numbers have increased around the ground, the crucial mark stats that previously grew for the club — contested marks, and marks inside 50 — have both dropped away.

A move away from marking forwards 2025 2026 Average marks 48.7 60.0 Average marks inside 50 7.3 5.0 Average contested marks 6.2 3.0

All of this comes with the caveat that the sample size is just two matches, but for teams to grow year on year, adding layers to their game style is crucial in staving off the planning of opposition sides.

Carlton has done just that with such a stark change to its ball movement and attack, but all of that adjustment up the field has been done with the same solid defensive base that made it so successful last year.

title: 'Backyard' e-bike battery repairs starting deadly fires, inquest told
text:
Lithium-ion battery fires are being caused by DIY e-bike alterations inspired by YouTube, an inquest has heard.

NSW Deputy State Coroner Kasey Pearce was overseeing the inquest in Sydney that was focused on the specific circumstances of four fires, two of which were fatal.

Videos from testing labs have been admitted into evidence, showing how hot and volatile the fires can get.

At least two of the fires, including a deadly blaze in Lake Macquarie, involved "backyard" repair jobs of e-bike batteries.

Judge Pearce's focus is on so-called micro-mobility vehicles, including e-bikes, e-scooters and hoverboards.

The inquest began in December and resumed this week.

Today, counsel assisting the coroner, Ann Bonnor, asked about repairs done by unlicensed people.

Andrew Low from Fire and Rescue NSW's Fire Investigation and Research Unit told the inquest that too often fires had been linked to homemade repairs or battery re-builds with parts bought online.

Fire and Rescue NSW has a special team to investigate and research battery fires. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

"There are backyard operations, they have soldering irons and they purchase things off eBay to do repairs," he said.

"Generally YouTube will show people how to do this [repairs] as well.

"Their exact motivations, I don't know, maybe whether to get more power, I am not really sure."

He said he had been to eight lithium-ion battery fires and most were linked to unauthorised repairs or people adding batteries to existing packs.

"I have been to a few where it has been evident that they have made some non-manufacture changes to batteries," he said.

His evidence echoed testimony given by Fire and Rescue Assistant Commissioner Brendan Cox in the initial hearing.

He said backyard repairers, purporting to be experts, had been linked to blazes in New South Wales and Victoria.

He said it was "unregulated and dangerous work, often sought after by people wanting to save money".

Fleeing fire

The first fire happened in short-stay accommodation at Cabarita Beach in Northern NSW in September 2023, a day after a man picked up his repaired e-bike battery.

He suffered severe burns to 40 per cent of his body, but survived.

In the second blaze being examined, a food delivery driver was injured in December 2023 when his second-hand e-bike battery exploded in his bedroom in the inner-Sydney suburb of Annandale.

Mazharul Haque Shohan, who suffered burns to 20 per cent of his body, gave evidence to the inquest today.

Three delivery drivers survived an e-bike battery fire in an Annandale unit in 2023. (Supplied: NSW Coroners Court)

Mr Shohan said he thought he was dreaming that night, before fleeing while on fire.

"I woke to a huge sound, I thought I was dreaming," he said.

"It was a matter of five seconds of my life, there was a really big bang and things were shaking."

He said there were flames and extra heat and he knew he had been burned.

"There were instant flames with the bang. The bang came out with a lot of sparks. Black smoke and smells," he said.

"It felt like it was blasting a couple of times."

Two other men fled the unit.

Mr Shohan told the inquest the month before he had his e-bike battery stolen, so he bought a replacement.

Explosions and death

The last two fires were fatal.

Patricia Kerr is one of two women who died in a house fire at Teralba, near Newcastle in 2024. (Supplied: Facebook)

In February 2024, two women died in a two-storey townhouse at Teralba, south of Newcastle.

The inquest heard a "backyard" repairer inserted mismatched pins and pierced an e-bike battery's casing before it exploded.

Patricia Kerr and Therese Harris were killed.

Therese Harris also died in the Teralba blaze. (Supplied: Facebook)

The inquest has heard temperatures could reach 900 degrees Celsius within minutes when lithium-ion batteries exploded.

The inquest heard battery cells could also be ejected from a battery pack up to 40 metres.

The two women died in a townhouse fire in 2024. (ABC Newcastle: Romy Stephens)

The fourth and final fire involved a battery charging 30 centimetres from the foot of a delivery driver's bed in Sydney last year.

The inquest heard he suffered incineration injuries, dying at the scene.

A bedroom that suffered significant fire damage after an e-bike battery overheated, resulting in the death of a man. (Supplied: Fire and Rescue NSW)

Fire Rescue NSW data tendered in court has said lithium-ion batteries caused about six fires in NSW per week.

The inquest is due to run until the end of next week.

title: Parents worry kids will inherit climate impact of coal mine extension
text:
As the independent referee weighs up one of NSW's largest mine extensions, parents are grappling with what the decision will mean for their children.

The Hunter Valley Operations (HVO) Continuation Project would result in mining continuing at the site near Singleton, in the Upper Hunter, until the end of 2045.

That would represent a 19-year extension of the Yancoal-Glencore joint venture's existing approvals, which expire in December.

HVO projections show the extension would allow an extra 429 million tonnes of coal to be mined, generating 809 million tonnes of CO2 emissions.

Activist group Parents for Climate today rallied against the project outside NSW Parliament House, with CEO Nic Seton saying he was "terrified" by the prospect.

Parents for Climate says the extension will negatively impact the next generation. (ABC News)

"My kids are in primary school now, and they haven't gone a year without being impacted [by climate change] in some way, whether that's being evacuated from a campsite or being sent to hospital for breathing too much bushfire smoke during the black summer," he said.

" I think a lot of other parents around the country are really worried about what the future of our society, our economy and our environment is going to look like for our kids. "

Mr Seton said he took no comfort from the HVO projection that about 98 per cent of emissions from the project would be Scope 3, or indirect, emissions produced when the coal was burnt by overseas buyers to produce electricity.

Nic Seton wants the extension to be rejected. (ABC News)

"It doesn't matter whether it gets burnt and transported locally or globally," he said.

"That pollution is still going to come back on people living all across the country in the form of extreme weather events, rising costs, disruptions of supply chains and food security.

"No-one's safe from it."

Job losses loom

But for Chris Bateman, a shift supervisor at HVO, a rejection by the IPC will come with a different type of social cost.

HVO employs more than 1,500 people and engages nearly 800 suppliers.

Chris Bateman says an extension of HVO would help secure his kids' futures. (Supplied: Chris Bateman)

"The Hunter Valley needs HVO," Mr Bateman said.

"It's massive in our community, most of my friends, if not all, are impacted either directly or indirectly by mining.

" Society itself is built around it. "

The former painter started at HVO about 15 years ago, working his way through the ranks.

He said the closure of the mine would impact thousands of children like his.

"I've been able to financially support us … we own our house, providing the kids with whatever they need to get through school," he said.

Hunter Valley Operations is one of the largest mines in NSW. (ABC News)

"HVO, and mining in general, provides a multitude of opportunities for our kids in apprenticeship programs [and] cadetships. It's also the fact that it's close to home, I'm able to come home every day and see my kids … [and] coach the football team."

Mr Bateman said both the climate and employment impacts of the extension were "valid things to consider" but HVO's current proposal continued to align with government requirements.

"The mine only equates to less than 1 per cent of NSW's annual emissions," he said.

"NSW mining is one of the most heavily regulated industries in the country as far as environmental constraints go, and we don't take that lightly.

" It's the community that we live in that we're doing it for, so we have as much, if not more, vested interest than anyone to make sure that we're doing it right. "

The IPC held two days of public hearings on the Hunter Valley Operations Continuation Project. (ABC Upper Hunter: Courtney Yeandle)

But Mr Seton said approving coal mine extensions placed an unfair burden on the next generation.

"By the time they grow up and get to vote, a lot of these decisions will have been made and it will be too late," he said.

" We need to be the adults in the room so the kids can count on us to make sure their future is as bright as possible. "

The IPC is expected to announce its decision on the future of HVO early next month.

title: Prime minister intervenes to guarantee refugee intake will not be cut
text:
The prime minister has guaranteed Australia's refugee intake will not go backwards, hours after his own cabinet minister confirmed plans to slash the humanitarian program by almost a third from next year.

In a dramatic intervention following a Labor backbench revolt over reports Australia would only take 13,750 refugees annually from next year, Anthony Albanese told the ABC the intake would remain at 20,000.

"The refugee intake needs to be renewed in the coming budget as the 20,000 places was available for four years," Mr Albanese said.

"This intake number remains government policy and will be continued in future years, consistent with Australia’s humanitarian commitments and sits beside our strong border security measures."

Earlier, a spokesperson for Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke confirmed Labor plans to reduce the humanitarian intake next financial year by 6250, as reported in the Australian Financial Review (AFR).

Mr Burke's office said Labor's decision to lift the intake in 2023 was always temporary and was only funded for four years.

But four Labor MPs, speaking on the condition of anonymity, have disputed this characterisation, telling the ABC they believed the higher intake was "enduring" and "not time-limited".

The proposed change has not been canvassed in any caucus forums, according to another MP, who said they expected the existing refugee intake to be maintained in line with Labor's National Platform when the funding comes up for renewal next year.

Last month at the ALP National Conference there was unanimous agreement on a resolution committing Labor to maintaining the intake at 20,000 per year "in the short-term" while continuing "to aspire to achieving" 27,000 places.

The issue has been described as "sacred" to party members, who have reluctantly accepted hardline border protection policies in exchange for the promise of Labor lifting Australia's refugee intake.

Speaking at the Daily Telegraph's Bush Summit in Dubbo today, Mr Albanese suggested the government was still finalising its policy.

Anthony Albanese cast doubt on the cuts despite confirmation from Tony Burke's office. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

When asked if Labor's crackdown on migration was in response to a populist push from parties such as One Nation, Mr Albanese said the government was responding "to the national need".

"There is a current spike in the support for One Nation, quite clearly," he said.

"But we've responded [to the migration issue] — we started lowering the numbers well before that occurred."

Employer wait for overseas nurses, teachers blows out Business leaders hope the current visa settings will be in place for 'a very short time'.

Australia has historically resettled a baseline of 13,750 refugees each year.

In 2022, the Morrison government temporarily boosted the intake to 17,875, for Afghan nationals, before then-immigration minister Andrew Giles announced a further increase to 20,000 per year in 2023.

At the time Mr Albanese said "the government will be tough on borders without being weak on humanity".

"When the Albanese government increased the refugee and humanitarian program to 20,000 places in 2023, there was no hint that this was a short-term increase," Refugee Council of Australia chief executive Paul Power said.

"If the cut goes ahead, the Albanese government would be implementing the policy Peter Dutton took to the 2025 election, turning its back on a commitment that has been Labor policy for 14 years."

Jana Favero says the reported cuts are an outrage and a betrayal. (ABC News: Erin Handley)

Asylum Seeker Resource Centre deputy chief executive Jana Favero said it was an "extraordinary betrayal" of Labor members who secured a commitment to maintaining Australia's refugee intake at its current level a month ago.

"I'm sure Labor MPs and members will be asking how a decision made openly and democratically at their own National Conference can be discarded so quickly by Anthony Albanese and Tony Burke," she said.

" This shows that they are panicking and it shows that One Nation is leading their migration policy. "

Lifting Australia's refugee intake has been embedded in the Labor party's platform for a decade.

The promise to resettle more refugees was critical in convincing Labor's left faction to endorse a number of hardline border protection policies, including boat turn-backs, at the 2015 ALP National Conference.

While a reduction in the refugee intake is not being considered as part of the government's looming migration overhaul, Labor is under pressure to reduce overseas arrivals and achieve its target of cutting net overseas migration (NOM) from the current 300,000 to 225,000 by 2028.

PM quells UK's backpacker visa concerns The prime minister has vowed not to make British backpackers work in regional areas as part of a looming migration overhaul, defusing a potential diplomatic stoush with the United Kingdom.

Mr Burke has already paused or slowed down the processing of Working Holiday Maker visas and bumped workers applying for skilled visas from overseas to the back of the queue.

As revealed by the ABC, the minister was also considering removing the favourable treatment of British backpackers, which would be in breach of the UK free trade agreement, before the prime minister intervened.

Mr Power said cutting 6,250 refugee places would have little impact on migration numbers, noting that the program overhaul has has contributed just 6.6 per cent to NOM over the past decade.

title: Plans to cool AI data centre using trucked-in water and rainwater
text:
A proposed AI data centre in north-west Tasmania plans to cool its facilities using rainwater and water that it trucks in.

Firmus Technologies wants to build a 52-megawatt AI data centre in Wesley Vale, at the old paper mill site in Mill Park.

The centre would produce AI tokens, needed for tools such as generative AI chatbot ChatGPT.

Latrobe Council has now released the project's development application, which is open for public submissions until September 9.

The council received the application months ago, but told the ABC it was waiting on Firmus to submit extra information before releasing it to the public and later voting on the proposal.

Earlier this week, George Town Council approved one of Firmus's other proposed data centres — a 288-megawatt facility in the Bell Bay Advanced Manufacturing Zone, in northern Tasmania.

Firmus is also building a 104-megawatt facility in the Launceston suburb of St Leonards.

Application details water use, noise emissions, jobs

Firmus came under scrutiny last month when it accidentally published information on its website about its water supply plans for the proposed Wesley Vale facility.

The company wrote that because there was no TasWater connection to the site, it planned to use rainwater and water from state-owned company Tasmanian Irrigation.

Tasmanian Irrigation supplies water to agricultural users and said at the time it could not legally provide water to data centres.

The development application shows Firmus now plans to use rainwater and water delivered by truck.

"We expect the trucking option to be needed only in extreme dry periods," the application states.

The AI data centre is proposed for the old paper mill site. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

The biggest water requirement is for cooling, which Firmus states will only be required on days when the temperature exceeds 26 degrees Celsius.

On noise emissions, an assessment published in the application found they would "not cause a significant loss of amenity or environmental nuisance", but recommended the assessment be updated when details were finalised.

"As the predicted combined noise level of the data centre is very close to the background + 5 dB(A) target level, it is recommended that additional noise mitigation measures are applied to the emergency generators to achieve a sound power level of 85 dB(A)," it states.

"This would allow for issues such as periods of unusually high noise propagation or equipment noise emissions that are higher than predicted by the manufacturer's catalogue data or that change over time."

The development application shows there will be 40 backup diesel generators at the site.

Council will vote whether to approve or reject the proposal after members of the public have their say. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Firmus said the Wesley Vale facility would support 70 jobs in construction and 20 ongoing roles.

The company does not yet have a power deal for the site, but has previously indicated its preference to use Tasmania's hydro energy.

"Firmus is committed to supporting new renewable energy projects in Tasmania, with the goal of fully matching the electricity demand of our sites over time," the development application states.

"We are only contracting energy that is available today, and are working with Tas Hydro to underwrite new energy as part of future contracting."

Planning scheme 'not fit for purpose' to evaluate data centres, mayor says

Latrobe Mayor Peter Freshney said the council's role was to assess the project against the planning scheme.

"It really does highlight the almost tension between the two roles of elected members — that is community representation and the role as a member of a planning authority," he told 936 ABC Hobart.

"The planning authority, and members therein, can only consider those components of a planning scheme that are applicable under the legislation.

"The community would expect us to consider much more than that."

Peter Freshney does not believe the planning scheme is the best way to assess AI data centres. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Some community members and councillors, including George Town Mayor Greg Kieser, believe Firmus's facilities should be assessed by the state government, rather than local councils under the planning scheme.

Cr Freshney said he did not believe the planning scheme, legislated in 1993, was fit for purpose to evaluate a project of this scale.

"It was legislated at a time when data centres as such would not have even been considered feasible or on the horizon," he said.

"I don't believe that any framework can be fit for purpose for every situation.

"I think there's an opportunity for both federal and state governments to reflect that concern, that reality."

Shane Wright cannot disguise his frustration at the unfair imbalance in the shonky GST arrangement between the federal government and the states and territories (“The dodgy deal hidden by bulldust”, August 27). That Western Australia is bestowed with much of the nation’s natural resources does not imply, nor should it ever have implied, that WA should enjoy a disproportionately larger part of the bounty from those resources than the rest of us. In vowing to continue the current arrangement, PM Anthony Albanese is following exactly the same game plan as he has done with the AUKUS accord: throwing good money after bad in the name of ruffling as few feathers as possible, and kicking the can down the road for others to deal with. He has sacrificed common sense for electoral security in the west and declared there would be no change to the GST arrangement while he is in office. It is a position that is refreshingly assertive, but thoroughly misguided. Bradley Wynne, Croydon Anthony Albanese has the back of Roger Cook … with a GST deal that is costing all of us billions of dollars. Alex Ellinghausen The carve-up of GST revenue favouring Western Australia is a joke, and the joke is on us. At least Albanese has provided the voters of the other states or his MPs with a potential remedy to the situation by declaring that “there would be no change to the system while he was prime minister”. Mind you, he used to say much the same thing about changing negative gearing and the capital gains tax, so who knows? Doug Walker, Baulkham Hills One limitation of democracy is that it can be difficult to make decisions that are both right and unpopular. Doing what is right can get you thrown out. That is why politicians do not make legal judgments. Imagine a trial when the judge must worry about being re-elected. We have set up independent bodies to decide electoral matters (AEC) and interest rates (Reserve Bank). It is time to set up a separate body to allocate state funding. If funding is essentially the GST, then a non-partisan body should decide where it is spent. Neville Turbit, Russell Lea Bravo, Cathy Wilcox Three Wilcox cartoons in a row encapsulate the big and important issues, from the environment and respect for women to justice and human rights. In a week in which the world has lost a secular saint in Dolly Parton, Cathy Wilcox’s work never loses sight of humanity and the need to do good things. Bravo Cathy. Colin Hesse, Nowra Photo: Cathy Wilcox

Trailing tech giants Twenty odd years ago, China realised that Arab oil would eventually become a problem and started to develop electric vehicles, which are now dominating EV sales in Australia. China’s emissions have peaked some six years ahead of their 2030 goal. Australia will not fulfil its climate change commitments, if we have any. Robots in China have apparently beaten the human 100-metre world record plus others at a recent event in Beijing (“Records tumble and so do robots at China’s humanoid Olympics”, August 26). Where is Australia in the robotics race? In the meantime, our Australian politicians have been debating hugely important matters, such as “melon-gate”, or arguing among themselves about themselves. Until we have credible, coherent, true leadership and vision from our politicians, Australia will continue to wallow in its own confused state, instead of maximising our undeniable potential. Mervyn Cross, Mosman Lies cost lives The fact that America is now experiencing an unprecedented measles epidemic and that children are dying was predictable from the moment that Trump, a charlatan, appointed Robert F. Kennedy jr, another charlatan, as secretary of health (“Measles kills two unvaccinated people as US outbreak approaches 3000”, August 26). There is no reason for anyone to persist in the belief that measles vaccination causes autism, a hoax that has been thoroughly debunked. The story starts with Andrew Wakefield, a British doctor who did much to cause the world to believe that mercury in tiny doses, thiomersal, was causing autism in children. He got an article published in The Lancet which made this claim. Subsequently, his co-authors renounced the article, it was shown to be based on falsified data, and he stood to personally make millions selling a test kit. The Lancet had to retract the article and Wakefield was deregistered in the UK for dishonesty and fraud but moved to America, where he is still treated as a hero by some people. When thiomersal was removed from measles vaccines in response to falling vaccination rates caused by this hoax, the rates of autism did not fall but kept rising, presumably due to increased awareness of the condition. Dr Ed Marel, Bathurst President Donald Trump holds an executive order about vaccines alongside Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy jun. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin Hikes hurt We are in the midst of a housing crisis. Construction companies are going bankrupt. We have already had three interest hikes this year to control inflation, placing a growing burden predominantly on families with young children (“Rate rise back on cards despite a step down in inflation”, August 27). The Reserve Bank could control inflation by adjusting the GST to target the entire population’s spending, rather than just punishing mortgage holders by raising interest rates. People with no mortgages keep spending freely when interest rates rise because these hikes do not affect them. Raising the GST rate would make everyday items more expensive and would immediately slow down consumer spending. Shifting the anti-inflation load to a consumption tax would protect people trapped in the housing crisis from endless mortgage rate hikes. The extra money collected from a higher GST could go to low-income households as cash rebates or cost-of-living payments. Lower interest rates make it easier for all people to afford a home and help mitigate the housing crisis. Please come up with a fairer solution to inflation than raising the official interest rate. Tony Martin, Glenwood

For them, the easiest way to solve a problem is to deny it exists. In the meantime, we destroy the planet and the future of our descendants. They will not remember us fondly. title: Powerhouse Parramatta chief Lisa Havilah departs just weeks from opening
text:
Advertisement

The opening of the billion-dollar Powerhouse Parramatta has been plunged into controversy after its chief executive stepped down 72 days before the opening of the state’s biggest cultural infrastructure investment since the Sydney Opera House. In a shock development, staff were alerted on Thursday afternoon that Lisa Havilah had stood aside from her role of seven years pending completion of a departmental investigation into “governance and procurement practices”. Only five days earlier, the museum had announced its first five exhibitions for the November 7 opening to much fanfare. CEO Lisa Havilah tours the new Powerhouse Parramatta. Janie Barrett NSW Government Architect Abbie Galvin has been appointed interim chief executive, and the former chief executive of Sydney Opera House, Louise Herron, as strategic adviser, starting Tuesday. Department secretary Melanie Hawyes sought to stabilise operations and committed to the opening timeline in a letter to staff: “As you would be aware from recent media reports, there is an ongoing investigation into matters relating to governance and procurement practices at the Powerhouse.

Advertisement

“After speaking with the chief executive earlier today, Lisa Havilah will be standing aside while the investigation is completed. “I recognise that this news comes at a significant time for the organisation, as we prepare for the opening of Powerhouse Parramatta. I know how much work, commitment and personal energy all of you have invested in reaching this milestone, and I want to assure you that there will be no impact to the existing programs of work, or the opening on November 7.” Havilah has been the single-minded driving force of the Powerhouse Parramatta since her appointment in 2019. The project aims to deliver western Sydney its first state-significant cultural institution, while redrawing Sydney’s cultural geography, and fundamentally changing how audiences encounter design, technology, and applied arts. But the new building has been bedevilled by political controversy over budget, location and heritage for more than a decade.

Advertisement

A protected whistleblower complaint around procurement practices and job appointments at the Powerhouse has been ongoing for almost a year, leading the Department of Creative Industries and Tourism to seek assurances from NSW Procurement in Treasury in March about the tender of museum contracts. Last month, the Herald published revelations that the museum had burnt through more than $70 million in the lead-up to its November 7 opening. The Powerhouse has spent more than $5 million on marketing and public relations in Australia and London, including $1.7 million-plus on a film and television documentary, as well as $25 million building exhibits for five opening shows, not including object loans, freight and commissioning of new artworks. Treasury parachuted Cassandra Wilkinson into the role of acting chief operating officer amid the spending disclosures. Arts Minister John Graham said Powerhouse Parramatta was on track for opening. “Following new allegations, the chief executive has stood aside while investigations into governance and procurement are finalised,” he said.

Advertisement

“I would like to thank the Powerhouse team for getting us to this point in the delivery of the Powerhouse Parramatta, the largest and most complex cultural infrastructure project since the Sydney Opera House.” Related Article City life Revealed: The five exhibitions to open the Parramatta Powerhouse The news took Parramatta Council by surprise, with the Lord Mayor Martin Zaiter declining to comment on Havilah’s departure. At the Powerhouse Parramatta offices on Thursday, workers told the Herald they were unaware of the developments and were cautious about commenting. One said the building was “pretty much done” and filled with “wonderful exhibits”. NSW Treasury secretary Michael Coutts-Trotter told budget estimates on Friday he was concerned about pre-opening overspending by western Sydney’s first cultural institution.

The Herald understands the museum’s board of trustees met two weeks ago to consider procurement issues at Parramatta. The museum’s executive was told at 2.30pm Thursday. title: ‘Thanks Miss Dolly’: Parton’s gift of books a legacy for children around Australia
text:
Advertisement

CultureCelebrityLiterature ‘Thanks Miss Dolly’: Parton’s gift of books a legacy for children around Australia Kerrie O'Brien August 27, 2026 — 5:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tears were shed around the globe after Dolly Parton’s death, but for some of the many children in Australia who have received the gift of books thanks to the US singer’s generosity, the news landed particularly hard. In south-west Victoria, seven-year-old Willow Board cried because she’d lost her hero, who had been sending her a book every month since she was born. Willow Board, 7, received books each month through Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, and got to speak to the singer via video link in 2023. Nicole Cleary “Thanks Miss Dolly,” Willow used to say each time she got a book from the letterbox. Those deliveries were thanks to the Imagination Library, Parton’s free book gifting program, established in 1995, which has delivered 300 million books to children all over the world.

Advertisement

When she was five, Willow was one of a handful of kids who got to meet Parton via video link. They talked about favourite books and the fact they both come from big families (Willow has six siblings). Parton spoke to every child. After hearing about Parton’s death, Willow said: “God would say she should be back on earth because she is a real-life angel.” Inspiration for the library, which gives a book a month to a child until they turn five, came from Parton’s own life – “my own dad who was not able to read nor write but was one of the smarter people one would ever want to know”. “Daddy was able to see [the program] take off and do good, and to hear the kids call me the book lady, he got such a kick out of that,” Parton said, adding that he considered it the best thing she ever did.

Advertisement

Related Article Vale How Dolly Parton became such a successful businesswoman – and why she said no to Elvis Every delivery comes with information about the story and its author, as well as ideas for parents to discuss with their child after they finish reading the book. Those tips are designed to help improve parents’ literacy, giving them skills teachers might use, such as encouraging the child to predict the story based on the cover or pictures within. The Imagination Library partners with Australian providers to deliver the program, including not-for-profit United Way, which has done so since 2013. United Way Australia CEO Lyndsey McKee says early literacy was identified as a clear need in Australia when the organisation became involved. “We knew that there was this wonderful program that was trusted and loved by many,” she says. “Those early years are absolutely critical.”

Advertisement

Around 50,000 children are enrolled currently in Australia, and more than 134,000 have taken part since its introduction. “The evidence is so significant around what a book in the home can mean for children in those critical years,” says McKee. “A child is 10 times more developmentally vulnerable if there is no reading at home.” How books are provided differs from state to state. In Victoria, United Way partners with kindergartens, while in NSW, it’s mainly through the Department of Education; local libraries are also often involved. About 70 per cent of the books are by Australian authors or illustrators, including about 10 per cent Indigenous creatives. Tanya Donovan whose children Victor, left, and Jamie take part in Dolly Parton’s library through the Glebe Treehouse in Sydney. Sam Mooy Helen Michael is a facilitator at Sydney’s Glebe Treehouse, a community centre that provides bridging programs between the community and schools. It runs playgroups for children aged zero to five, with about 101 kids registered for the Imagination Library, including about 55 First Nations families. A huge fan of the concept, Michael says even five minutes of shared reading time makes a big difference. As well as helping literacy, research shows how powerful that is in that time together helps bonding, calms the child’s nervous system, exposes them to early learning and, longer term, helps prevent low self-esteem around literacy, which will improve socio-economic outcomes. It’s so powerful, she says, it may start as something as simple as a little nursery rhyme between a parent or foster parent, but it has a huge impact.

Advertisement

South-west Victorian teacher Grace Greenham, mother of Hazel, 3, and Hugo, 10 months, agrees – her daughter has been receiving a book each month through the Imagination Library since she was a baby. “Hazel is at the age now where getting mail is very exciting for her, especially when it’s a book with her name on it,” she says. Hazel Greenham, 3, is part of the Imagination Library program. Nicole Cleary “Hazel is only three but we’ve read to her since she was born and even as a 12 or 18-month-old she would sit down with us on our laps and ask for a story. When it’s something you start from such an early age it becomes part of their everyday life and something they really look forward to.” In her work as a teacher, Greenham sees firsthand the impact of reading at home. “I notice a huge difference in the classroom of students who have been read to consistently, not only in their ability to pick up reading and language skills quickly but also in their vocab when they are speaking as well.

title: Why NSW Health is reviewing equipment contracts after safety concerns

The NSW government is investigating what options it can enforce under a contract that locks the state’s ambulance fleet into using error-plagued defibrillators for a further six years. The Therapeutic Goods Administration has temporarily banned the corpuls3 and corpuls3T defibrillators from sale while they investigate reports the devices unexpectedly shut down and reboot during use. NSW Health Minister Ryan Park told budget estimates he would review the government’s contract with the beleaguered defibrillator’s manufacturer. NSW Parliament The government has maintained that the devices are safe for use and that the TGA’s advice had “no current impact” on operations. Healthcare Defibrillators in our ambulances randomly shut down, TGA admits He told budget estimates on Thursday that the TGA had not indicated they planned to recall the devices, but said he was concerned about the issues raised and would “have a look at the contract and what options there are for us”. “When a company goes into contract with us and we provide them with taxpayers’ money, then they have to provide a service that meets that. I’m concerned that a number of paramedics have said to me that the device is not doing that now.” An Australian Paramedics Association survey found 96 per cent of respondents had experienced problems or fault with the corpuls device, and half (48 per cent) said it could have affected patient care.
