"We weren't clearly told where they were going to take us. When we first saw the authorities' ship, I thought they were going to take us to Australia," Farid tells SBS News.

Instead, he was taken to Naoero (formerly known as Nauru), where he would spend years caught up in Australia's newly established offshore processing system before eventually returning to Afghanistan.

"It was like a camp. We get our turns, about once a month, to go out for a few hours," he says.

Farid, a pseudonym, was 17 when he was rescued by the MV Tampa in August 2001, alongside 432 other asylum seekers. Source: SBS News

"For the first year we didn't get to go out at all. We were not very hopeful. It was just tents at first, but then they set up portable rooms," Farid says.

Today, he is 42 and lives in Melbourne's south-east, where he works as a painter after completing trade courses and an apprenticeship. He was granted asylum in Australia in 2012.

The ordinary life Farid has built in Australia is a long way from the journey that brought him here, one that began when he was a teenager fleeing Afghanistan and led him into the centre of the 'Tampa crisis' and Australia's emerging offshore processing system.

Twenty-five years on, his experience offers a human window into the events surrounding the Tampa and the policy that followed, known as the Pacific Solution, as Australia continues to debate how it responds to people seeking protection.

When the Tampa answered the call

On 24 August 2001, the Palapa ran into trouble in rough seas about 140km north of Christmas Island, leaving those on board facing the prospect of sinking.

Two days later, on 26 August, Australia's Rescue Coordination Centre alerted ships in the area that the vessel was in distress, with the words "HELP" and "SOS" painted across its roof.

The closest vessel was MV Tampa, whose captain, Arne Rinnan, agreed to come to their aid. Guided by an Australian Coastwatch aircraft, the Tampa reached the stricken fishing boat and began taking those on board to safety.

The Tampa affair unfolded in August 2001, after the vessel rescued 433 asylum seekers from a sinking fishing boat before being prevented from reaching Christmas Island. Source: SBS News

For Farid, the rescue should have marked the end of a terrifying journey. Instead, it was followed by a confrontation that would reshape Australia's approach to asylum seekers arriving by boat.

Rinnan initially headed towards the ferry port of Merak, Indonesia, but several asylum seekers reportedly pressured him to take them to Australia instead. According to a subsequent Senate inquiry, some threatened to jump overboard or hurt themselves if they were taken to Indonesia.

Fearing for their safety, Rinnan changed course for Christmas Island.

Australian authorities refused permission for the vessel to enter Australian territorial waters and directed Rinnan to take those aboard to Indonesia.

The Palapa was carrying more than 400 asylum seekers when it became stranded on 24 August. Source: AAP / Wallenius Wilhelmsen

As the standoff continued, Rinnan raised concerns about the deteriorating health of some passengers.

Australian authorities arranged for food, water, and medical assistance, but the deadlock continued.

On 29 August, Rinnan declared a state of emergency and sailed into Australian waters without permission, prompting the government to send 45 Special Air Service (SAS) troops to board the vessel.

Farid remembers the arrival of the authorities as another moment of fear.

"I was nervous and frightened because they [authorities] wore face coverings and had their fingers on the trigger."

It was like seeing something in the movies. We were confused because the captain explained to us that he was not permitted to enter into Australian waters.

Christmas Island caught in the middle

Gordon Thomson was a Christmas Island Shire councillor at the time and had direct contact with Rinnan during the standoff, including through fax.

Gordon Thomson, a Christmas Island Shire councillor at the time, led a rally calling for the Tampa refugees to be allowed to land on Christmas Island in August 2001. Source: Supplied

On 28 August 2001, Thomson and other elected representatives issued a statement calling on the then-prime minister John Howard to allow the Tampa into the island's port.

"We applaud the captain and crew of the Tampa for their correct application of humanitarian principles and the law in taking onto their ship asylum seekers by offering safe refuge on Christmas Island," the statement read.

But a day later, as the government moved to prevent the Tampa from reaching the island, Thomson says the atmosphere on Christmas Island changed.

"The government brought in the SAS, armed boats and attack craft, effectively taking control of and, in many people's eyes, pirating the Tampa and forcing it back out to sea," he tells SBS News.

"They also closed the port, which meant local people couldn't go out on the water. No-one was allowed to get into a boat, despite fishing being a daily necessity for many people on Christmas Island."

International journalists and news crews gathered on Christmas Island amid intense global interest in the August 2001 Tampa standoff. Source: Supplied

"The government was determined that journalists couldn't get onto boats and reach the Tampa to tell their stories. There was a real clampdown on movement across the island," Thomson says.

With the standoff unresolved, the government turned to an alternative: those aboard would be taken elsewhere, where their claims for protection would be processed.

Life in Naoero

Hassan Ghulam was a community elder in Australia when nearly 300 asylum seekers were transferred to Naoero in September 2001.

Naoero is a tiny Pacific island nation about 3,000km north-east of Australia, and had a population of roughly 12,000 people at the time.

In the weeks after the Tampa crisis, Australia reached an agreement with the Naoero government to establish an offshore processing centre at Topside, in the island's remote interior. In return for hosting the asylum seekers, Naoero received financial and development assistance from Australia.

Community leaders like Hassan Ghulam became crucial links to those on Naoero, advising the Hazara refugees and gathering information about life inside the camp. Source: SBS News / Supplied

The centre was still being built when the first arrivals were sent there, with many initially housed in large tents while Australian personnel worked to establish the facility.

As more asylum seekers arrived, Topside quickly became crowded, with conditions marked by extreme heat, water shortages and limited electricity.

From Australia, people like Ghulam became crucial links to those inside, advising the Hazara refugees and gathering information about life inside the camp from journalists and detainees via satellite phone.

When they were taken on the boat [to Naoero], the conditions were terrible and many suffered from severe physical distress.

"What they endured throughout felt like it was a punishment to scare them into coming into Australia … it was [also] a message intended to the [people] smugglers," Ghulam says.

The now 75-year-old says smugglers charged large sums to put people on boats that were often poorly equipped and unseaworthy, with water sometimes flooding into the vessels as they crossed open seas.

"We Hazaras are mountain people, not sea people," he says.

"If you leave us on a mountainside, we can climb like goats. But in the sea, we are not fish — we would drown."

The first Naoero facility was established rapidly in the aftermath of the crisis, and accounts from the period describe difficult conditions, including shortages of water and other basic services. The island's remoteness also meant limited access to medical care and other support.

Ghulam says he made several attempts to reach Naoero, including one with an Australian documentary news crew hoping to record the conditions inside the detention centre, but they were stopped before they could even board the plane.

Letters from limbo

Instead, detainees began sending Ghulam letters from Naoero — some describing the harsh living conditions, others sharing their hopes for the future, and many reflecting on the pain of being separated from the people they loved.

The letters that made their way from Naoero painted a picture of lives suspended in uncertainty.

In one dated 27 October 2002, a detainee wrote of the ongoing water shortages: "Sometimes God helps us, rain is a great source of water, people come out of containers and take bath in the rain."

They also described the emotional toll of being separated from family: "Normally I do not like to think of my sisters because such feelings make me upset and weak and the circle of life becomes slower here."

SBS News has seen some of the letters, but has not independently verified them in their entirety.

Elaine Smith, an advocacy worker who worked closely on the Tampa affair in Australia at the time, also reviewed copies.

The letters also show some detainees trying to maintain hope despite their circumstances.

One wrote that he did not want to burden the person receiving his letters with his troubles, saying he wanted to "share" his joys.

He described starting a small mathematics class for fellow detainees, while teaching himself English grammar and fiction from the Naoero library.

He said those were among the few subjects available, unlike the mathematics and physics he wanted to study, and asked whether he could pursue further education by distance.

The politics of the Tampa

On 1 September 2001, Howard announced that Naoero and New Zealand had agreed to receive the Tampa passengers for refugee-status processing outside Australia. The arrangement became the foundation of what was later known as the Pacific Solution.

The Tampa's arrival came just weeks before Australia's federal election, which was shaping up around issues including border protection and asylum seekers.

Government figures showed boat arrivals had risen sharply in the years before the Tampa affair — from 921 in 1998-99 to 4,137 in 2000-01. The Howard government argued that Australia was being "targeted by organised people smugglers" because its "refugee determination outcomes were overly generous".

Then-prime minister John Howard poses for a photograph with a couple in the federal seat of Ryan in March 2001, during the federal election year. Source: AAP / Dave Hunt

At the launch of his 2001 election campaign in Sydney, Howard famously delivered a line that would come to define his political legacy on border protection: "We will decide who comes to this country and the circumstances in which they come."

In a sit-down interview with SBS News 25 years later, he continues to defend his approach and says he reflects positively on his immigration policies.

We were ahead of our time … you couldn't maintain domestic support for strong immigration policies if you allow people to come willy-nilly to live in our country.

"What we adopted was a common sense approach. You cannot maintain local support for high immigration if people feel that the government no longer controls either the number of people or who they are."

Children overboard controversy

The Howard government's hardline approach to boat arrivals reshaped Australia's border policy, but also gave rise to some of the most controversial episodes of the 2001 campaign, including the "children overboard" affair.

The controversy centred on events surrounding SIEV 4, a vessel intercepted by the Australian Navy's HMAS Adelaide on 6 October 2001, about 100 nautical miles north of Christmas Island.

The following day, 7 October, a report emerged that asylum seekers had thrown children overboard as the Navy attempted to intercept the vessel. A subsequent Senate inquiry found no children had been thrown overboard from SIEV 4.

On 8 October, SIEV 4 started to sink while under tow, and photographs taken during the rescue were later presented as evidence associated with the alleged incident.

The inquiry found the photographs had been wrongly associated with the "children overboard" claim.

Howard has previously defended his handling of the affair, saying he relied on the advice he received at the time. In 2002, he told ABC Lateline he had never been told the original advice was wrong. Twenty years later, in an interview with the Guardian, he again defended the claims, saying: "It was the advice we had at the time."

Former prime minister John Howard told SBS News there had been a "miscommunication" in the advice he received during the "children overboard" controversy. Source: SBS News / Alexandra Jones

But in his interview with SBS News 25 years on, Howard offers a somewhat different characterisation of the episode.

That was a mistake, that was a miscommunication.

"I don't think anybody is to be blamed for that," he says.

He says the reaction was understandable given the "enormous turmoil" and emotion of the time, before shifting focus to what he sees as the policy's longer-term outcome.

"All I can say is it's good we are not having accidents at sea now, like we used to have then."

The legacy of 'stopping the boats'

Howard's reference to "accidents at sea" points to the deadly period of boat arrivals that followed the Tampa affair.

In December 2010, 50 people died when SIEV 221, carrying asylum seekers, crashed into the rocky shoreline of Christmas Island in treacherous seas — a tragedy the WA coroner later described as the largest loss of life in an Australian maritime incident in peacetime in 115 years.

It was one of a series of boat journeys in the years that followed, with hundreds of asylum seekers dying at sea as boats attempted to reach Australia.

A protest sign on Christmas Island calling for the Tampa refugees to be allowed to land, reading: "Let the Tampa refugees land." Source: Supplied

Since December 2013, the Australian government has reported no known deaths at sea from maritime people-smuggling ventures targeting Australia.

Howard views that outcome as evidence that Australia's approach was ultimately vindicated — and argues that other countries are now confronting similar challenges.

We were right and the rest of the world is adopting our approach.

Howard says the position he took during the 2001 election was criticised at the time, particularly by some Europeans who regarded it as insensitive. But, he argues, many of those same countries are now grappling with the challenges of irregular migration and border control.

"You can't have an open, tolerant, non-discriminatory immigration policy if it's open slather," he says.

"You can't. And we decided a long time ago. And the rest of the world is now adopting the approach we adopted then."

The challenges Howard describes remain evident across Europe. On 21 August, French police were filmed intercepting an inflatable boat as migrants attempted to cross the English Channel to Britain, part of an intensified effort to prevent small-boat departures.

At the end of July, thousands of people tried to cross from Morocco into Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta, in a mass influx that resulted in dozens of deaths.

Asked how he would judge his own legacy on immigration and border protection, Howard declines to do so himself.

"That's for other people. I cannot be my own judge. Others will be my judge.

"I think we ran an immigration policy that most Australians support, one that still allows us to adopt a humanitarian approach."

The debate over 'stopping the boats'

Graham Thom, advocacy coordinator at the Refugee Council of Australia, acknowledges immigration is a complex issue, but disagrees offshore processing was responsible for 'stopping the boats'.

"One of the key myths that is very difficult to dispel is that somehow offshore processing stops the boats from arriving," he tells SBS News.

Graham Thom, advocacy coordinator at the Refugee Council of Australia, says offshore processing has not stopped people arriving by boat. Source: AAP / Bianca De Marchi

"There's this whole narrative around 'stopping the boats', when what we saw after Tampa was the Howard government starting to intercept boats and push them back," Thom says.

Tampa didn't stop the boats. People kept coming.

"Until we acknowledge that the Pacific Solution had nothing to do with stopping the boats, we're sort of trapped in a system that has bipartisan support for cruelty."

Thom says Australia should instead work with countries across the region, including Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand, to ensure people have basic rights, access to work and study, and protection from detention or removal while longer-term solutions are found.

"[We] don't need to resettle everyone," he says.

"As long as there is hope that those most at risk can get to some sort of safety, then you remove the incentive for people to get on dangerous boat journeys."

When asked about critics who argue that the arrival of asylum seekers by boat is not Australia's responsibility, Thom says the issue needs to be considered as part of a broader global system.

"I say to any critic, we are part of a global system and we have to look at our responsibility globally.

"If we don't solve the problem at its source, people are going to keep moving, and they will keep moving until they find safety and security.

Demonising, criminalising and isolating people is not the solution.

Thom says the debate over border protection has continued to shape how migration is discussed in Australia.

Protesters dressed as SAS troops mark the second anniversary of the Tampa affair at a rally in Melbourne in 2003. Source: AAP / Joe Castro

"I think the whole migration debate is blowing up on all proportions and it is always easy when times are tough to blame someone … and migrants are often first to face those attacks," Thom says.

"Ultimately, how we treat them is a reflection of us, not a reflection of people trying to seek a better life."

Howard rejects that characterisation of his approach. He says he hadn't been concerned with how the decision might be viewed 25 years later; he was thinking of "what's right at the time" and that "we had to say no".

"We have a proud record of taking people in from all around the world and a generous humanitarian program.

"We wanted to maintain that."

Life after Tampa

But Naoero was not the end of Farid's story. His asylum application was rejected and he was eventually returned to Afghanistan, where he lived for eight years before being granted asylum and returning to Australia in 2012.

Today Farid is a painter, but his hopes of pursuing a career as an educator have not disappeared.

Since leaving Afghanistan, he has helped establish a primary school of 320 students in his old village, a dream he has relished, having grown up determined that no other child in his community would have to travel hours to reach the nearest school.

Farid's life now straddles two places: the community he left behind in Afghanistan and the life he has built in Australia. His experience offers a personal lens into a question at the heart of Australia's migration debate: what does it mean to become Australian?

Howard views it differently, rejecting the idea that Australia's identity needs to be defined as either "mono" or multicultural.

"It's all pointless. I don't think we should fret about definition, what it is.

The thing is, migration to Australia since World War Two has been a huge success.

"[But] what we should not do is ignore people who want greater control over immigration. They want a ceiling on the number of people who come here, and they don't want people who aren't willing to adopt our ways coming here. How you enforce those two things is a matter of debate."

title: 'You can't escape': A growing fight over what belongs in Australia's suburbs
text:
In Brief New federal government rules will ban future data centres from being built near homes and schools.

But residents living alongside them say they've been left out and feel powerless.

When Sean Brown moved to West Footscray two years ago, days after his son was born, he thought he'd found a good spot to raise a family — green space, a train station nearby, and a community with room to grow.

Instead, his home is now 300 metres from one of the largest data centres in the country.

"It's a massive black box in the middle of a residential area. There's this visual heaviness to it that you can't really escape," Brown told SBS News.

NextDC's M3 facility in the Melbourne suburb brings a constant humming noise audible even 100m away, he said, while ongoing construction means near-constant light, noise and disruption.

Parking is scarce with facility workers competing for street spots, and Brown said whole streets have lost power for full days at a time during infrastructure works, with little warning and no compensation. He's also worried about health risks, and the future of his entire suburb.

Sean Brown lives 300m away from one of Australia's biggest data centres. Source: Supplied

Branded by its chief executive, Craig Scroggie, as "Australia's largest hyperscale AI factory", the M3 site is set to double in size by 2027 — covering 10 hectares in size, and drawing 225MW of power, 24 hours a day.

A separate facility, the Perri Melbourne Data Centre (PMDC), has been approved and planned just a few blocks over.

There are currently 162 operational data centres across Australia, with a further 90 proposed, according to the Climate Council — and it's unclear whether planned rules to data centres in residential areas will apply to any of them.

In the streets of West Footscray surrounded by houses, a "massive black box" has taken over. Source: Supplied / Sean Brown

Government crackdown on new data centres

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese used a speech to the Business Council of Australia's annual dinner on Tuesday night to announce new national rules that would block future data centres from being built near homes, schools, or prime agricultural land.

READ MORE The new plan to prevent data centres from driving power prices up

Developers will also be required to add more renewable energy to the grid than their data centres consume, minimise water use, and ensure new sites are appropriate for their size — avoiding land that could otherwise be used for housing.

"Australia is in a strong position to attract investment in data centres, but maintaining social licence will be essential," Albanese said.

"That means ensuring energy bills do not rise, water security is maintained and locations are appropriate."

Asked about communities already living with data centres, Albanese did not directly answer when pressed on ABC Perth on Tuesday, instead pointing to the same social licence framework.

Asked by SBS News whether any measures would target existing sites or address community concern that the new rules don't cover people already affected, the prime minister's office declined to comment.

NextDC's M3 data centre is set for an expansion that will cover 10 hectares of West Footscray, while another separate facility, the Perri Melbourne Data Centre (PMDC) has been approved just a few blocks over. Source: Supplied / Sean Brown

A big gap

While Brown welcomes the changes in principle, he said they don't reach the people already living with the consequences.

"If it doesn't fix the problems that have been caused in West Footscray, what's the point of it?" Brown said. "This community's just been completely sold down the river if we're not looked after. Why do our children continue to bear this risk?"

He's sceptical that the sites would have been approved under the new government frameworks and said it needs to expand to existing data centres, not just the new ones.

"If areas where they've already been inappropriately built are just left to fend for themselves, how is that fair at all?"

Associate Professor Dr Ehsan Noroozinejad, a researcher at the Urban Transformations Research Centre at Western Sydney University, welcomed the government's changes but said a clear gap remained.

"The proposed rules mainly shape future development, so they do not automatically resolve concerns around existing facilities," he told SBS News.

The M3 site is set to double in size by 2027 — covering 10 hectares in size, and drawing 225MW of power, 24 hours a day. Source: Supplied / Sean Brown

"Communities already living near data centres need clear standards for noise, water use, backup generators, traffic and energy impacts, backed by transparent monitoring."

Noroozinejad said Australia still needs data centres, but problems arise when they aren't put in the right places with the right infrastructure.

"It's important not to assume every data centre creates the same problems," he said. "The real issue is performance, location, and whether costs are shifted onto the surrounding community."

Dr Michael Vardon, from the Fenner School of Environment and Society at Australian National University, said the deeper problem is procedural: communities have almost no input before a facility is approved.

"This is about where new facilities go, and setback rules do not apply retrospectively," Vardon told SBS News.

"The approval comes first, the community finds out afterwards, and by then the only remaining policy lever is the operating conditions."

A view of NextDC's M3 data centre from Kendal Coombs' house. Source: Supplied / Kendal Coombs

Olivia Shen, director of the strategic technologies program with the United States Studies Centre at the University of Sydney, said a key provision of the changes will be whether they apply to both expansion of existing data centres as well as new projects.

"Many data centres have operated in Australia for decades, often without the surrounding community even realising they are there," Shen told SBS News. "However, if existing data centres are allowed to expand to a point where they encroach on homes, schools and agricultural land, then this becomes a bit of a policy loophole."

'We feel really powerless'

Another West Footscray resident, Kendal Coombs, bought a house four years ago about 200 metres from the M3 site, when the block was still vacant.

She said she was initially told by council that the site was going to be a "business park", but realised a few months after moving in that it was a data centre — which was initially not a concern until its rapid expansion.

"We're all angry and concerned but it's hard to know what to do, we feel really powerless," she said.

"These projects destroy communities. If they're making these determinations [that future data centres can't be built near homes or schools] because it is too unsafe or too much of a risk to our health to live near them, then they need to pay reparations to the residents affected."

Brown said the centres have made it harder to sell up and leave.

"There's a lot of people here who are really angry about what impact this is going to have on their house prices — because I sure as hell wouldn't live near a data centre," he said. "I wouldn't buy this house."

He's pushing for compensation: voluntary housing buybacks at competitive market rates for those who no longer want to live there, relocation costs covered for owners and renters alike, and payment for disruption already endured.

NextDC has not responded to these proposals, Brown says, adding government intervention is needed.

Both Noroozinejad and Vardon say more transparency and reporting is needed for existing data centres in neighbourhoods — particularly information around water and energy use, noise, independent monitoring, and a complaints register.

Practical measures such as acoustic upgrades, landscaping, traffic management and limits on backup-generator testing can also help, Noroozinejad said.

But for Brown, it might be too late.

"They've just killed this area now," he said. "We're witnessing the death of a suburb."

NextDC declined to comment.

title: 'Extraordinarily expensive': Is this Australia's most controversial construction project?
text:
In brief Victorian Premier Ben Carroll says changes to the Suburban Rail Loop will mean it is "built under budget".

There has been division over the infrastructure project's costs, with the state Opposition vowing to review it if elected.

Few infrastructure projects have generated as much debate as Victoria's Suburban Rail Loop.

The 90km rail project promises to reshape how Melbourne grows and moves, but its cost, benefits and delivery timeline have been fiercely contested.

That debate has again been thrust into the spotlight after Premier Ben Carroll announced $2 billion in cuts to the project this week, declaring: "I respect your money."

Supporters say the rail loop is a once-in-a-generation investment that will help accommodate Melbourne's growth. But critics argue it comes with an eye-watering price tag and uncertain returns, helping make it one of Australia's most controversial infrastructure projects.

Liam Davies, a lecturer in sustainability and urban planning at RMIT University, said the SRL was a step towards transforming Melbourne's city-centric public transport system into an interconnected network.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Melbourne's greatest challenge is that it has become an extraordinarily large city, physically," he told SBS News.

"We can't just adopt the transport strategy for a denser, more compact city like London. We need to do something of our own, and the SRL is an attempt to do that in a Melburnian context."

With Labor and the Coalition deeply divided on the SRL, the project's future could be decided when Victorians head to the polls in November.

Why is the project so controversial?

The SRL will connect Melbourne's middle suburbs from Cheltenham in the south-east to Werribee in the west via Melbourne Airport through a 90km underground rail line.

The project is split into three stages. The first section — SRL East — is under construction, running from Cheltenham to Box Hill via six new underground stations. The first trains are expected by 2035.

Critics argue the mega-project's business case doesn't stack up, and the multi-billion-dollar price tag is a financial liability for Victoria, which has the second-highest debt per capita of any state or territory, behind the Northern Territory.

The project's first stage, SRL East, in Melbourne's south-east is well underway. Source: Supplied / Victorian government

More than $33 billion has already been invested in SRL East, according to the premier.

A Parliamentary Budget Office analysis puts the price tag for building the East and North sections at $96.4 billion, though there is currently no fully costed estimate for the entire project, which includes the final stage, SRL West.

An evaluation last year by Infrastructure Australia — an advisory body to the federal government — found the SRL's business case was insufficiently detailed and relied on future stages to justify its benefits.

It also urged the Victorian government to develop "exit strategies" should the project be unable to be completed.

Allegations of corruption and unlawful conduct in state-funded projects, which recently led to a royal commission into the construction industry being called, have also heightened public concerns about the SRL.

Davies said there are questions about which other infrastructure projects will miss out on investment because of the SRL.

"This is still an extraordinarily expensive project," he said.

"Is this the only project that we build over the next 35 to 50 years, or do we build other projects at the same time?

"If it's the only project that we build, I don't think it's the best allocation of resources."

Are there alternatives?

Carroll, who replaced Jacinta Allan as premier last month, has clearly recognised that many Victorians are unhappy with the eye-watering cost.

On Tuesday, he announced $2 billion in savings, with underground station interchanges at Box Hill and Glen Waverley no longer to be built, instead replaced by surface transfers.

Among other changes, a second station entrance will not be built at Clayton, and pedestrian bridges in Burwood and Cheltenham have also been axed.

"I respect your money," Carroll said in a statement.

"The SRL will be built on time. Today's changes mean it will be built under budget."

Davies said construction of SRL East was well advanced, with tunnel boring machines in place to begin excavating twin 26km tunnels.

"The reality is that that project is so far along; it will continue," he said.

But it's the project's latter stages which have scope for change.

Davies said better rail services and upgrades to the northern and western suburb lines, including electrification of the entire track, would fulfil many of the policy ambitions of SRL West at a fraction of the time and cost.

"We have an exploding population in our northern and western suburbs, and the infrastructure is not keeping up at all," he said.

He said there could also be alternatives to the SRL North, such as elevated rail, light rail, or a rapid bus transit system with dedicated bus lanes.

"There are challenges to each of those options; each of them has trade-offs," he said.

"All of them would be cheaper options than what we currently have, which is tens of billions of dollars in tunnelling."

Where do the parties stand?

The project's future could hinge on the outcome of the state's November election.

Labor has committed to seeing the SRL through, arguing it's essential infrastructure for a growing Melbourne.

The state Opposition has previously called for the project to be scrapped, arguing that it's too costly and the funds should be redirected to other, higher-priority transport projects, such as a long-sought-after airport line.

In 2024, Liberal MLC Evan Mulholland described the SRL as a "vanity project" that was "robbing the next generation of getting the infrastructure that they deserve".

But the Coalition's position has evolved over time, with Opposition leader Jess Wilson now promising to pause and review the project if elected.

Whatever the outcome, the project will remain a defining political issue for years to come.

"Transport projects are big and expensive, and they almost always have controversy," Davies said.

"It's almost impossible to build something that everyone is going to be absolutely happy with. Maybe this is just another example of that."

title: 'Get it out': ARIA to ban AI-generated music from Australian charts
text:
In brief ARIA will ban fully AI-generated music from featuring on its charts from Friday.

Australian artists like Peking Duk's Adam Hyde have welcomed the move.

Music will need to be "substantially human-made" in order to qualify for Australia's main music chart, in an industry bid to stamp out AI-generated tracks.

Songs wholly generated using artificial intelligence will no longer be eligible for the ARIA charts from Friday, in an update to The Australian Recording Industry Association's (ARIA) code of practice.

ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd said a chart that rewards unlicensed AI output would "undercut the very basis of the recorded music we exist to present".

"The ARIA charts are about tracking consumption and sales of music in Australia, but they're also about celebrating human artistry and success," Herd told ABC radio.

"We're not particularly interested in including AI-generated music as part of that process, particularly when it's taking up a spot from an Australian artist in the chart."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

AI-assisted songs will still feature on the charts, but they must be substantially human-made and raise no stream or chart manipulation concerns.

"I'm sure that there are a lot of artists that are using AI tools to enhance creativity, to do really cool, new, exciting things," Herd said.

"Artists have always been at the forefront of new tech ... it's made some of the best music ever created, and no doubt AI will create some really exciting evolution of that."

Songs on the ARIA charts that use AI include Gold Coast-based DJ and producer Josh Fawaz's dance track Like a Prayer, which is fourth on the ARIA's top 20 Australian singles after peaking at number two in May.

A dance cover of Madonna's 1989 hit, generative AI is credited for the drums and vocals on the track, according to Spotify.

Australian electronic band Peking Duk supported the association's call to outlaw generative AI from the charts, claiming it was "removing the human experience from life".

"AI is using our stuff. It's using a lot of our peers' stuff, you know, people we know," band member Adam Hyde told Channel Nine's Today show.

"There is so much good art in Australia and something like AI coming along and kind of sweeping the charts and all that jazz, it's like, get it out."

ARIA's decision heeds global AI principles drawn up by the record industry's peak body, The International Federation of the Phonographic Industry, in July.

The federation said the guidelines would be rolled out to official charts in Latin America, the Middle East, Africa and Southeast Asia and advocated to more than 20 other official chart programs in Europe and the Pacific, including the ARIAs.

title: Trump's visa crackdown plan could affect thousands seeking asylum in the US
text:
In brief The US government is set to revoke business and tourism visas for foreigners seeking asylum.

If enacted, it would be the largest mass revocation of visas in US history.

The Trump administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum status in the United States.

If it happens, the move would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history and would likely face legal challenges.

Unless challenged or revised, the US state department is expected to announce in the coming weeks the revocation of so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum, according to state department documents obtained by the Associated Press (AP) and two US officials. The action will be taken in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

"We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently," state department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said.

He declined to comment on the number of visas that might be revoked, saying "as the process will be ongoing, the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis".

The revocations would not necessarily result in their immediate deportation, the officials said. Most of those with asylum cases currently pending would be recategorised but would lose their status as business or tourism travellers, according to the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the revocations are not final yet.

Since US President Donald Trump took office for his second term last year, his administration has steadily ramped up restrictions on visa applicants — demanding more information about their social media histories, requiring the posting of expensive bonds to process visas, and outright banning the issuance of visas to citizens of certain countries.

In a social media post on Tuesday, US deputy secretary of state Christopher Landau called out people who he said try to use tourist and business visas to get into the US and then apply for asylum.

"People in the US and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims," Landau said in a post on X. "Asylum isn’t supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law."

Landau cited the case of a Colombian citizen who came to the US in 2015 on a tourist visa and then applied for asylum.

B1 visas are generally issued for business trips and B2 visas are generally issued for tourism, family visits or medical care. It was not immediately clear from the documents or the officials how many of these visa holders are seeking or have sought asylum in the US and would be affected by the revocations.

Current applicants for B1 and B2 visas are asked to affirm that they will not apply for asylum in the US and prove that they intend to return to their home countries.

In the past 18 months, the state department has revoked about 175,000 visas for people who have been convicted or accused of crimes ranging from drunken driving to rape and robbery, as well as for people who have spoken out publicly against US policies, particularly in the Middle East.

The administration has also moved to crack down on so-called birth tourism, a practice the administration claims is used by foreign pregnant women to come to the US to give birth so that their child will benefit from birthright citizenship.

Trump has tried several times to end birthright citizenship, but those challenges have been rejected by courts, including the US Supreme Court.

The state department documents obtained by AP suggest screening of current B1 and B2 visa holders began after the state department received information about asylum requests from the US Citizenship and Immigration Services.

title: Powerhouse Parramatta chief Lisa Havilah departs just weeks from opening
text:

The opening of the billion-dollar Powerhouse Parramatta has been plunged into controversy after its chief executive stepped down 72 days before the opening of the state’s biggest cultural infrastructure investment since the Sydney Opera House. In a shock development, staff were alerted on Thursday afternoon that Lisa Havilah had stood aside from her role of seven years pending completion of a departmental investigation into “governance and procurement practices”. Only five days earlier, the museum had announced its first five exhibitions for the November 7 opening to much fanfare. CEO Lisa Havilah tours the new Powerhouse Parramatta. Janie Barrett NSW Government Architect Abbie Galvin has been appointed interim chief executive, and the former chief executive of Sydney Opera House, Louise Herron, as strategic adviser, starting Tuesday. Department secretary Melanie Hawyes sought to stabilise operations and committed to the opening timeline in a letter to staff: “As you would be aware from recent media reports, there is an ongoing investigation into matters relating to governance and procurement practices at the Powerhouse.

Advertisement

“After speaking with the chief executive earlier today, Lisa Havilah will be standing aside while the investigation is completed. “I recognise that this news comes at a significant time for the organisation, as we prepare for the opening of Powerhouse Parramatta. I know how much work, commitment and personal energy all of you have invested in reaching this milestone, and I want to assure you that there will be no impact to the existing programs of work, or the opening on November 7.” Havilah has been the single-minded driving force of the Powerhouse Parramatta since her appointment in 2019. The project aims to deliver western Sydney its first state-significant cultural institution, while redrawing Sydney’s cultural geography, and fundamentally changing how audiences encounter design, technology, and applied arts. But the new building has been bedevilled by political controversy over budget, location and heritage for more than a decade.

Advertisement

A protected whistleblower complaint around procurement practices and job appointments at the Powerhouse has been ongoing for almost a year, leading the Department of Creative Industries and Tourism to seek assurances from NSW Procurement in Treasury in March about the tender of museum contracts. Last month, the Herald published revelations that the museum had burnt through more than $70 million in the lead-up to its November 7 opening. The Powerhouse has spent more than $5 million on marketing and public relations in Australia and London, including $1.7 million-plus on a film and television documentary, as well as $25 million building exhibits for five opening shows, not including object loans, freight and commissioning of new artworks. Treasury parachuted Cassandra Wilkinson into the role of acting chief operating officer amid the spending disclosures. Arts Minister John Graham said Powerhouse Parramatta was on track for opening. “Following new allegations, the chief executive has stood aside while investigations into governance and procurement are finalised,” he said.

Advertisement

“I would like to thank the Powerhouse team for getting us to this point in the delivery of the Powerhouse Parramatta, the largest and most complex cultural infrastructure project since the Sydney Opera House.” Related Article City life Revealed: The five exhibitions to open the Parramatta Powerhouse The news took Parramatta Council by surprise, with the Lord Mayor Martin Zaiter declining to comment on Havilah’s departure. At the Powerhouse Parramatta offices on Thursday, workers told the Herald they were unaware of the developments and were cautious about commenting. One said the building was “pretty much done” and filled with “wonderful exhibits”. NSW Treasury secretary Michael Coutts-Trotter told budget estimates on Friday he was concerned about pre-opening overspending by western Sydney’s first cultural institution.

The Herald understands the museum’s board of trustees met two weeks ago to consider procurement issues at Parramatta. The museum’s executive was told at 2.30pm Thursday. Public Service Association of NSW, representing staff, has written repeatedly to Arts Minister John Graham about the “excessive use of external labour and consultants”, and urged an independent financial audit of the spending and recruitment methods used by senior management at the Powerhouse. title: ‘Thanks Miss Dolly’: Parton’s gift of books a legacy for children around Australia
text:
Advertisement

CultureCelebrityLiterature ‘Thanks Miss Dolly’: Parton’s gift of books a legacy for children around Australia Kerrie O'Brien August 27, 2026 — 5:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tears were shed around the globe after Dolly Parton’s death, but for some of the many children in Australia who have received the gift of books thanks to the US singer’s generosity, the news landed particularly hard. In south-west Victoria, seven-year-old Willow Board cried because she’d lost her hero, who had been sending her a book every month since she was born. Willow Board, 7, received books each month through Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, and got to speak to the singer via video link in 2023. Nicole Cleary “Thanks Miss Dolly,” Willow used to say each time she got a book from the letterbox. Those deliveries were thanks to the Imagination Library, Parton’s free book gifting program, established in 1995, which has delivered 300 million books to children all over the world.

Advertisement

When she was five, Willow was one of a handful of kids who got to meet Parton via video link. They talked about favourite books and the fact they both come from big families (Willow has six siblings). Parton spoke to every child. After hearing about Parton’s death, Willow said: “God would say she should be back on earth because she is a real-life angel.” Inspiration for the library, which gives a book a month to a child until they turn five, came from Parton’s own life – “my own dad who was not able to read nor write but was one of the smarter people one would ever want to know”. “Daddy was able to see [the program] take off and do good, and to hear the kids call me the book lady, he got such a kick out of that,” Parton said, adding that he considered it the best thing she ever did.

Advertisement

Related Article Vale How Dolly Parton became such a successful businesswoman – and why she said no to Elvis Every delivery comes with information about the story and its author, as well as ideas for parents to discuss with their child after they finish reading the book. Those tips are designed to help improve parents’ literacy, giving them skills teachers might use, such as encouraging the child to predict the story based on the cover or pictures within. The Imagination Library partners with Australian providers to deliver the program, including not-for-profit United Way, which has done so since 2013. United Way Australia CEO Lyndsey McKee says early literacy was identified as a clear need in Australia when the organisation became involved. “We knew that there was this wonderful program that was trusted and loved by many,” she says. “Those early years are absolutely critical.”

Advertisement

Around 50,000 children are enrolled currently in Australia, and more than 134,000 have taken part since its introduction. “The evidence is so significant around what a book in the home can mean for children in those critical years,” says McKee. “A child is 10 times more developmentally vulnerable if there is no reading at home.” How books are provided differs from state to state. In Victoria, United Way partners with kindergartens, while in NSW, it’s mainly through the Department of Education; local libraries are also often involved. About 70 per cent of the books are by Australian authors or illustrators, including about 10 per cent Indigenous creatives. Tanya Donovan whose children Victor, left, and Jamie take part in Dolly Parton’s library through the Glebe Treehouse in Sydney. Sam Mooy Helen Michael is a facilitator at Sydney’s Glebe Treehouse, a community centre that provides bridging programs between the community and schools. It runs playgroups for children aged zero to five, with about 101 kids registered for the Imagination Library, including about 55 First Nations families. A huge fan of the concept, Michael says even five minutes of shared reading time makes a big difference. As well as helping literacy, research shows how powerful that is in that time together helps bonding, calms the child’s nervous system, exposes them to early learning and, longer term, helps prevent low self-esteem around literacy, which will improve socio-economic outcomes. It’s so powerful, she says, it may start as something as simple as a little nursery rhyme between a parent or foster parent, but it has a huge impact.

South-west Victorian teacher Grace Greenham, mother of Hazel, 3, and Hugo, 10 months, agrees – her daughter has been receiving a book each month through the Imagination Library since she was a baby. “Hazel is at the age now where getting mail is very exciting for her, especially when it’s a book with her name on it,” she says. Hazel Greenham, 3, is part of the Imagination Library program. Nicole Cleary “Hazel is only three but we’ve read to her since she was born and even as a 12 or 18-month-old she would sit down with us on our laps and ask for a story. When it’s something you start from such an early age it becomes part of their everyday life and something they really look forward to.” In her work as a teacher, Greenham sees firsthand the impact of reading at home. “I notice a huge difference in the classroom of students who have been read to consistently, not only in their ability to pick up reading and language skills quickly but also in their vocab when they are speaking as well.

The NSW government is investigating what options it can enforce under a contract that locks the state’s ambulance fleet into using error-plagued defibrillators for a further six years. Healthcare Defibrillators in our ambulances randomly shut down, TGA admits He told budget estimates on Thursday that the TGA had not indicated they planned to recall the devices, but said he was concerned about the issues raised and would “have a look at the contract and what options there are for us”. “When a company goes into contract with us and we provide them with taxpayers’ money, then they have to provide a service that meets that. I’m concerned that a number of paramedics have said to me that the device is not doing that now.” An Australian Paramedics Association survey found 96 per cent of respondents had experienced problems or fault with the corpuls device, and half (48 per cent) said it could have affected patient care. The devices are used in about a third of the state’s local health districts, a senior NSW Health official told budget estimates, as well as in about 1600 ambulances across the state. NSW Health Secretary Susan Pearce said her department had begun extensive contingency planning, and was considering the supply and availability of other devices on the market. “It’s incumbent upon us to be prepared for a worst-case scenario with respect to a TGA-ordered withdrawal of those devices ... we can’t continue on as though that’s not a possibility,” she said.

NSW Health Deputy Secretary Matthew Daly said there would not be a procurement lag, as the department had identified appropriate devices from suppliers in the US, which could be directly freighted: “We could move very quickly.” Pearce said the TGA had not indicated a recall was likely, but if one happened the department had been assured it would not be rushed: “An abrupt withdrawal would be very dangerous.” “[The] health system would require time ... to properly roll out any new device.” Australian Paramedics Association NSW president Brett Simpson said the most time-consuming part of the rollout would be training paramedics in a new device.

An author who claimed Hollywood giant Disney lifted the plot of its latest Indiana Jones film from her book has failed to overturn her defeat in the copyright battle. Lucasfilm She argued a District Court judge was wrong in March this year to find Indiana Jones and the Dial of Destiny did not infringe on her copyright. The judge made “factual errors” in failing to find parts of the 2023 film were “identical” to her 2021 novella The Michelangelo Dilemma: Secrets of Renaissance Time Travellers, Gane told the appeal justices.

Gane’s 4000-word, 21-page novella is available as a $9 e-book from Amazon. “Because I’m the mother of the primary work so for me it’s like a newborn,” Gane said. “I see them as a particular feature like the same bone structure.” Gane claimed Disney had taken 13 original elements from her work such as the Ancient Greek mathematician Archimedes inventing a time-travel device and concealing it in his tomb. “Archimedes’ tomb linked to time travel is unprecedented,” Gane said.

Court of Appeal president Debra Mullins also questioned the claims relating to historical details. “I don’t think Archimedes saying ‘eureka’ is original,” Justice Mullins said. Long-range forecasts by the NSW government show the state’s population will rise by 3.4 million between now and 2066, economic output per person will increase by 35 per cent over that period and residents will live longer, healthier lives. The five-yearly NSW Intergenerational Report, which gauges how demographic change will affect the state over the next 40 years, says population growth will slow from its current rate of 1.1 per cent a year on average to 0.8 per cent. That will result in NSW reaching 12 million people by 2066, up from 8.6 million. The NSW population is forecast to reach 12 million by 2066. Louie Douvis Overseas migration will be the main driver of population growth. But the contribution of natural increase (births minus deaths) will decline – it will account for 10 per cent of annual population growth in 2065-66, compared with 26 per cent in 2024-25.

Advertisement

People in the state will have fewer children and have them later in life. The NSW fertility rate – the expected number of births per woman – is expected to drop to 1.35, far below the “replacement rate” of 2.1 needed for a stable population. During the past 40 years, life expectancy at birth in NSW has climbed from 76 years to 83 years on average. That trend will continue, albeit at a slower rate; the report predicts life expectancy to reach 89 years by 2066 (over 90 years for women). The ageing of the population will exert increasing influence on society and economy. The share of people aged 65 will rise from 18 per cent today to 25 per cent by 2066.

Economic output per person in NSW, now about $97,000, is forecast to rise to $131,000 by 2066 (when measured in 2023-24 dollars). The 2026-27 intergenerational report, prepared by NSW Treasury, says climate change will reshape economic activity and affect the way people live and work. “More extreme weather and harsher environmental conditions will affect industries unevenly, requiring adaptation across sectors – from infrastructure and land use to health and productivity,” the report says. Artificial intelligence is expected to boost productivity over the medium to long run, allowing companies “to generate higher profits, offer higher wages and reduce prices for customers”. It is also likely to “transform” labour markets.

“However, the magnitude and timing of these effects are uncertain,” the report says. Labour productivity is forecast to grow by 0.8 per cent per year in NSW over the next 40 years, well below the rate forecast in previous intergenerational reports (1.2 per cent in 2021 and 1.5 per cent in 2016). This downgrade follows more than a decade of sluggish productivity improvement in NSW and Australia. The workforce will increase as a share of the population over the next 15 years because of longer working lives and stronger participation by women. But during the 2040s participation will begin to decline.

Advertisement

“By the 2040s, population ageing is likely to become the most important structural force affecting participation and average hours worked per person,” the report says. Related Article Ageing Older Sydney town: the suburbs where the over 65s outnumber those under 20 Previous intergenerational reports have projected a long-term fiscal gap as government spending outstripped revenue due to the demands caused by a rapidly ageing population. But this report shows that fiscal gap has been almost entirely closed, narrowing from 2.6 per cent of gross state product in 2021-22 to 0.1 per cent. Even so, the report warns government finances in NSW will still face “sustainability challenges”. Gross state debt is projected to rise from about 19 per cent of gross state product (GSP) in 2024-25 to 90 per cent after 40 years. This compares with a long-term projection of gross debt reaching 133 per cent of GSP in the previous intergenerational report.

Treasurer Daniel Mookhey said the report showed the state’s outlook is better than it was five years ago. “While our disciplined approach of paying down debt and responsibly managing expense growth is having an impact, this report shows there’s still more work to be done,” he said. The Australian sharemarket had its biggest slump in 12 weeks as bets firmed for another interest rate rise as early as next month and investors digested another flood of results from companies including Qantas and Wesfarmers. The S&P/ASX 200 fell 89.60 points, or 1 per cent, to 9038.20 on Thursday, with all 11 sectors in the red bar healthcare and industrials. The losses came after the bourse fell 0.4 per cent on Wednesday as shock inflation figures put another rate hike on the table. Wall Street drifted through a quiet session overnight after a report showed US inflation was also worse than expected. Wall Street didn’t provide a lot of direction for the ASX. Bloomberg Expectations of another rate rise by the Reserve Bank firmed after the Australian Bureau of Statistics said on Wednesday underlying inflation in July had unexpectedly risen by 0.5 per cent. The gauge most watched by the RBA had been forecast to ease, but instead remained steady at 3.6 per cent. The hot inflation data spurred economists from Goldman Sachs to Commonwealth Bank to predict another rate increase as early as next month, abandoning calls of no change for the remainder of the year. CBA, the nation’s biggest lender, said this morning the inflation data would cause the RBA to “lose patience” and predicted a quarter-point hike to 4.6 per cent – the highest level in 15 years – in November, with the risk of a move at next month’s meeting.

Deutsche Bank’s Phil O’Donaghoe, who was first to change his call after the data, went further and forecast a hike at the September meeting, saying underlying inflation is “intolerably high”. National Australia Bank’s Sally Auld also switched to calling a September hike, with the risk “biased towards an additional hike in November, especially if activity data shows resilience in coming months”. Rising interest increases borrowing costs for consumers and companies, weighing on company profits and share prices. Sectors dependent on consumer demand and tech companies borrowing heavily to grow are among those vulnerable to rate hikes, while banks – while often seeing a short-term boost to profit margins – can be hit by a rise in loan defaults and bad debts. Earnings season Qantas boss says air traffic delays at Sydney Airport ‘not OK’ Financial stocks finished the session lower, with CBA down 0.3 per cent, NAB down 0.7 per cent, Westpac up 0.4 per cent and ANZ Bank down 1.3 per cent. Tech stocks also pulled lower, with software makers Xero and WiseTech down 2.6 per cent and 3.3 per cent respectively, and AI data centre operator NEXTDC down 1.6 per cent. Real estate investment trusts struggled, too, with Goodman Group losing 0.7 per cent, Westfield shopping centre landlord Scentre falling 1.4 per cent and property developer Stockland slumping 3.7 per cent. Gold producers weighed on mining stocks as gold prices eased over the spectre of rising rates, which typically reduce the appeal of non-yielding gold as an investment. Evolution Mining lost 1.4 per cent and Newmont shed 1.9 per cent. Iron ore and copper giants BHP and Rio Tinto dropped 1.5 per cent and 0.5 per cent. Consumer staples also declined, with Woolworths (down 1.6 per cent) and Coles (down 1.2 per cent) giving back some of their gains from the past session.

On the corporate earnings front, Qantas climbed 4.8 per cent after flagging revenue growth of 8 to 10 per cent for the current year, helped by higher fares. Its profit in the past financial year took a hit as rising fuel costs from the war in the Middle East outpaced the benefit of sustained demand for international travel. The airline posted a 13.8 per cent fall in underlying pre-tax profit to $2.06 billion in the year to June, in line with analyst estimates, as its fuel bill jumped by more than $600 million. Rival Virgin Australia benefited from Qantas’ tailwind, lifting 6 per cent. Related Article Earnings season Why Kmart’s next furniture showroom won’t be in a big capital city Wesfarmers fell 4.6 per cent after posting a 1.8 per cent fall in net profit to $2.87 billion. The retail conglomerate’s sales rose 3.4 per cent to $47.3 billion, and profits excluding significant items grow by 8.3 per cent to $2.9 billion. The company said Bunnings boss Mike Schneider would retire in February, with chief customer officer Rachel McVitty to take the helm. Healthcare giant Sigma slumped 7.8 per cent, with investors underwhelmed by its first result since taking over Chemist Warehouse. Sales jumped 15.5 per cent to $10.8 billion and profits climbed 22.3 per cent to $732.2 million. Sales at Chemist Warehouse were boosted by demand for weight-loss drugs, which will help lift revenue by double digits again in the current financial year, Sigma said.

Mayne Pharma shares lost 1.6 per cent after saying its underlying full-year earnings slumped 27 per cent to $34.2 million as management was distracted by the $672 million takeover bid by US private-equity backed drugmaker Cosette, which was eventually blocked by Treasurer Jim Chalmers on national interest grounds. “The Cosette transaction process and subsequent legal matters placed real demands on management focus and caused general disruption,” CEO Aaron Gray said. Ramsay Health rallied 13.7 per cent after the hospital operator said its net profit jumped 19.3 per cent to $364.1 million, helped by tighter cost management, a focus on therapeutic areas such as cardiology, orthopaedics and cancer care, and growth in hospital admissions. On Wall Street overnight, yields in the bond market, the focus of Wall Street’s biggest recent worries, edged higher following America’s inflation data, weighing on sentiment. The S&P 500 edged down by less than 0.1 per cent and remains near its all-time high set this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 113 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.1 per cent. Nvidia, the chipmaker at the heart of the artificial intelligence boom, delivered a sales forecast that met expectations. Its shares were up 4.3 per cent in after-hours trade.

Though analysts had forecast $US105.2 billion on average, some projections exceeded $US110 billion, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Strong profit growth across US companies broadly has been the main reason the US stock market has run to records this year. Abercrombie & Fitch leaped 35.7 per cent after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The retailer also raised its forecast for earnings over the full year and for how much cash it will send to investors by buying back shares of its own stock. Outside of earnings reports, Meta Platforms added 1.1 per cent after agreeing to pay up to $US18 billion ($24 billion) and to add child-safety measures to Facebook and Instagram to end a landmark trial over teen social media addiction and settle claims filed by states across the country.

In the bond market, US Treasury yields ticked higher to 4.65 per cent from 4.64 per cent late on Tuesday following updates on inflation and economic growth. Yields had shot upward through the American summer on worries about high inflation and the US government’s gargantuan debt, among other factors. They got so high that the US Treasury Department made a surprise announcement last week to intervene in the bond market, though analysts say its effect could be limited. Related Article Opinion

That was the same rate of inflation as in June and slightly worse than the 3.6 per cent that economists expected, according to FactSet. It remains far worse than the 2 per cent goal the Fed has set. Traders are betting on a nearly three-in-four chance the Fed will hike the federal funds rate at least once by the end of the year, according to data from CME Group. One of the factors that’s worsened inflation this year is higher oil prices, though they’ve come down recently.

title: Fears for 'lovely' Australians missing in Nepal flood
text:
Dozens of Australians are missing in deadly flash flooding in northern Nepal, including a "lovely" group of family friends undertaking a sacred pilgrimage.

Almost 1500 people are unaccounted for and at least 165 have died since a wall of mud and rock collapsed into a river near the Himalayan border with China.

Among the missing are at least 34 Australians, including 15 who were undertaking a trek with US travel company Himalayan Glacier Adventures.

Rescuers are scrambling to save survivors after an avalanche of ice and rock triggered floods. (AP PHOTO)

Vasan Srinivasan, who knows 14 Australians on the 13-day tour, said the group were family friends completing a sacred pilgrimage together.

Advertisement Advertisement

"Hopefully we find them somewhere safe ... I'm just praying every minute," the Confederation of Indian Australian Associations chair told AAP.

The Hindu Indian families from Sydney and Melbourne were active community members who frequently volunteered for causes including mental health awareness.

"They are lovely families, the kids are all studying and they are all very connected to the community," Mr Srinivasan said.

"I'm a bit shaken up, they are 14 of my close family friends."

Earlier on Thursday the tour operator said it had not been able to contact anyone from the group, which included two boys aged 11 and 14, because of damage to mobile networks and electricity infrastructure.

Advertisement Advertisement

Chief executive Sagar Pandey flew by helicopter to "personally observe the situation and aid with rescue" but was unable to land becaujse of conditions on the ground, the company said.

Scores of ‌bodies have been recovered from floodwaters. (AP PHOTO)

The tour group took off from Kathmandu on Sunday for a 13-day trek to the sacred Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar on the Tibetan Plateau.

Photos posted on social media in recent days showed the Australians smiling upon arrival at Kathmandu Airport and receiving safety briefings.

The Himalayan Glacier website lists "possible landslides on the Nepal side" during tours in August.

Officials at Nepal's tourism ministry told media outlets 340 foreigners were among more than 400 tourists missing after the disaster.

The cause and toll of the natural disaster are yet to be confirmed, but footage and witness accounts are adding to a picture of the flood's devastating path.

The cause and the death toll from the devastating flash flooding are yet to be determined. (AP PHOTO)

Some communities tried in the seconds they had to warn people downstream of the impending flood, University of Sydney disaster management expert Soniya Rijal said.

"People were informing their relatives and neighbours via call saying, 'the flood is coming, please be careful, evacuate'," she told AAP.

"However, people did not believe it because it wasn't raining. They thought they would be okay."

Dr Rijal survived the 2015 Nepal earthquake and said she could only imagine the panic being felt by those in the disaster zone.

"I think this situation is a little different, but the panic would be similar," she said.

The Nepalese Embassy in Canberra said efforts to locate and rescue those affected, and assess the full extent of human casualties and damage, were ongoing.

Dr Rijal said the Nepalese Army would respond to the disaster and had deployed helicopters to assist in the early stages.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese urged Australians in the affected area to follow the advice of local authorities, adding officials were working to confirm their welfare.

Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade personnel were being deployed to the region, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said.

title: Aussies left 'in fear' as suburbs transformed around the country: 'Popping up everywhere'
text:
Angry residents are raising the alarm over Melbourne's booming AI data centre industry, leaving local councils to grapple with mounting concerns over the massive developments appearing across the city's west.

Brimbank has joined other western councils calling for a pause on new data centres and expansions while the long-term impacts of the rapidly growing industry are investigated.

Mayor Virginia Tachos told Yahoo News Australia councils were worried the state government was rushing into a once-in-a-generation infrastructure build without properly understanding what concentrating data centres will mean in 10, 20 or 30 years.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"We want to see a rigorous process to understand the demands on the land, water, electricity and supporting infrastructure - all that needs to be considered," she said.

Tachos also questioned what would happen to the enormous facilities if technological advances allowed the same computing power to be housed on much smaller sites.

"What do we do with those data centres? How do we decommission them? We want to know what footprint will they leave behind," she said.

"The residents have told us flat and clear they don't want them in their neighbourhoods."

NEXTDC's M3 data centre in West Footscray is one of the large-scale facilities operating in Melbourne's west, as councils raise concerns about the growing demands of data centres on power, water, land and surrounding communities. The facility provides infrastructure for cloud computing, AI and other digital services. (Michael Dahlstrom)

Residents raise concerns over 'heat island effect'

Tachos said residents had raised concerns about heat, noise, diesel storage and the enormous amounts of water and electricity required to operate data centres.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"I think there's a lot of fear in the community at the moment because people are worried about the heat island effect," she said.

The concern is particularly significant in Melbourne's west, where large expanses of roads, roofs and concrete absorb and retain heat while a lack of tree cover reduces natural cooling.

Victorian Government mapping found Brimbank was among Melbourne's hottest municipalities, recording an average summer urban heat island effect of more than 9.5C, while parts of the municipality were given the highest possible heat-vulnerability rating.

There is also emerging evidence data centres can increase surrounding temperatures, with a recent US study finding neighbourhoods downwind of four facilities were 0.7C to 0.9C warmer on average, with increases of up to 2.2C recorded.

Brimbank is among Melbourne's hottest municipalities. (Victorian Government)

'The west has always been' Melbourne's dumping ground

The backlash has also reignited a longstanding grievance that Melbourne's west has repeatedly been expected to accommodate the infrastructure and industries needed by the rest of the city.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"The west has always been seen as a destination for landfills and dumping all the rubbish," she said.

"We've had to live with the aftereffects of contamination and a lot of brownfields.

"Now, data centres are popping up everywhere."

The scale of proposed developments has also added urgency to concerns as councils fear they can be sidelined from major planning decisions.

Data centres are already operating across Brimbank and neighbouring suburbs, while several more are proposed, including Syncline's planned 350-hectare Victorian AI Hub at Plumpton, which would be the country's largest.

Tachos said councils weren't trying to stop investment but wanted a "seat at the table" to ensure the consequences for communities were properly considered before more projects were approved.

RELATED:

Data centres are large facilities filled with computer servers that store, process and transmit the vast amounts of digital information used to power cloud services, websites and increasingly artificial intelligence.

How will Australia regulate data centres?

The concerns come as National Cabinet moves to tighten oversight of the industry, agreeing to develop mandatory national standards covering data centre energy and water use, land use and skills and training, with Commonwealth legislation planned for early 2027.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Planning Institute of Australia CEO Matt Collins shared the sentiment of council, saying the decision recognised the need to carefully manage where large data centres are built.

"A poor location can place additional pressure on electricity and water systems, compete for scarce land, require costly infrastructure upgrades and erode community confidence," he said.
